k.p: Even the robust defenses of theism lose to naturalism once you get into the details.
l: Fine-tuning is taken seriously by plenty of non-theist philosophers, and naturalism's main replies are an unobservable multiverse or brute fact.
Naturalism wins on points, and its answer to fine-tuning is still "a lot of universes."
The naturalist's reply to fine-tuning is infinite universes, which is plenty of faith.
Something can't come from nothing. There's something. So someone made it. That's the whole debate, and it was over before philosophy departments existed.
Atheism is cope.

k.p: Giving up a core commitment of classical theism to escape an objection means the objection worked.
k.b: Dropping a doctrine means you lost
l: Traditions revise under pressure without that counting as defeat. Science does it routinely.
Revising a doctrine in response to an argument is what you'd want from anyone.
By that standard, physics has been refuted about forty times.
Theology has changed its answers for two thousand years and it's still here. Things that are false don't last two thousand years. So changing the answers is how you can tell it's true.
Aquinas already answered that. He numbered it.

k.p: A sane believer resists the question "if God commanded something monstrous, would you do it?" Only a pathological one just says yes.
k.b: Sane believers resist 'what if God commanded it'
l: Resisting the question is a way of rejecting divine command theory while keeping the vocabulary.
If the believer checks the command against a prior sense of good, that sense is doing the work.
The sane believer has a morality and a God, in that order.
God is good by definition. So He couldn't command anything bad. So the question is like asking what if a triangle had four sides, and only atheists think it's clever.
Without God, "wrong" means "I don't like it."

k.p: The Catholic God, of all gods, being the real one would be a nightmare.
k.b: The Catholic God would be a nightmare
l: The doctrine of hell is hard, and Catholic theology has centuries of work on reconciling it with mercy and freedom.
Finding it frightening isn't an argument that it's false.
"I'd hate it if it were true" is a review.
A true thing doesn't care whether you'd enjoy it. People only say a view would be a nightmare when they suspect it's right.
Thomism is the most consistent system ever built.

k.p: Call-in show atheism is garbage. The serious debate is with theistic philosophers of religion.
l: The philosophers of religion are mostly believers defending what they already held, which is a selection effect worth weighing.
A field where nearly everyone started out agreeing with the conclusion.
Philosophy of religion is the home game.
The apologists have read more than the atheists and win every debate. Winning debates is how you find out who's right. So that's that.
Analytic philosophy of religion is Christians with logic notation.

k.p: Stalinism was a vulgar corruption of the doctrine. It doesn't follow from Lenin.
l: The one-party state, the Cheka and the ban on factions all came before Stalin. The tools were built under Lenin.
Stalin inherited the equipment. He didn't invent it.
The corruption used the original machinery without modification.
Stalin was Lenin's general secretary, in Lenin's party, under Lenin's rules. If a student does exactly what the teacher set up, that's the teacher.
Lenin and Stalin are the same. One died sooner.

k.p: The Bolsheviks never promised to abide by bourgeois elections, so dissolving the Constituent Assembly was no betrayal.
k.b: Dissolving the Assembly wasn't a betrayal
l: They campaigned for the Assembly and closed it after losing. "We never promised" is a narrow defense.
They ran in the election. That's usually taken as agreeing to it.
It wasn't a betrayal, they just lost and shut it.
An election is whoever gets the most votes. They got fewer. In every other context that's called losing, and here it's called a higher form of democracy.
Democratic centralism is "we vote and then I decide."

k.p: A party with a fixed ratio of intellectuals to workers was a principled design.
l: A party that sets its own ratio of thinkers to workers has decided in advance who does the thinking.
Workers in the majority, and the minority writes the program.
One intellectual per ten workers, and guess who talks.
If the workers could lead themselves there'd be no need for a party. There's a party. So the theory already assumes they can't, and everything after follows from that.
The vanguard party is "trust me bro" with a reading list.

k.p: You have to read Mandel, Kliman and the rest before you get an opinion on this.
l: A position that can only be assessed after thousands of pages of in-house literature is hard to tell apart from one that can't be assessed.
The reading list grows every time the argument goes badly.
"You haven't read enough" has never lost a debate.
If it were true, it could be explained in a paragraph. Physics can do it. This needs forty books, and that means even the authors weren't sure.
Forty books to explain why the revolution didn't happen? That's retarded.

k.p: Marx expected the workers' state to be short and healthy, with revolution in the advanced countries first. What happened isn't on him.
l: The predictions failing is evidence about the theory. A theory isn't cleared by having expected something else.
"He didn't know what would happen" is the criticism.
The theory was fine. Events did it wrong.
Marx predicted the revolution in England. England got fish and chips. A scientist whose experiment fails every time isn't unlucky.
Marx was wrong, and Lenin proved it by trying.

k.p: Middle-class radicalism corrodes working-class cohesion.
l: Class politics and identity politics have often reinforced each other. The union movement's best decades included civil rights.
The working class has identities too. Treating them as a distraction has lost elections.
The workers were meant to be united, apart from the things they care about.
The working class is whoever works. Most people work. So everyone's working class, and the term picks out nobody.
Woke is just Marxism with race swapped in for class. Everyone knows this.

k.p: The working class is still the agent that matters.
l: Organized industrial labor is a shrinking share of the workforce in rich countries. The agent the theory needs is hard to find.
The proletariat was meant to have nothing to lose. It got a mortgage.
The revolutionary subject has a pension and a pickup.
Workers vote for whoever they like, and lately it isn't the left. If the workers are always right, they're right about that too.
Workers don't want the means of production, they want Fridays off.

k.p: Even the less unhinged right-wingers are peddling the same ruling-class idealism.
k.b: Even the sane right is ruling-class ideology
l: Calling every opposing view ruling-class ideology means no argument from that side ever has to be answered.
"That's ideology" is a reply that works on everything, including itself.
Everyone who disagrees is a dupe of the ruling class, which is handy.
If every idea comes from a class, so does Marxism. Marx was middle class and lived off a factory owner. So Marxism is bourgeois ideology by its own test.
Marx was a capitalist. He lived off Engels' factory.

k.p: Fascistic currents in the ruling class are the more dangerous ones right now.
k.b: The fascist wing is the danger
l: "Fascist" has been applied so widely that it's lost much of its power to pick out what's new.
Every right-wing government since 1945 has been called fascist by somebody.
The boy who cried Mussolini.
Fascists wore uniforms and marched. Nobody's marching. If it doesn't have the uniform, it's something else, and something else isn't as scary.
Communists and fascists are the same people at different ages.

k.p: The labor theory of value holds up when you read it properly.
l: The transformation problem is a real difficulty, and a century of rival solutions suggests the trouble is in the theory.
It needs a new interpretation every decade to stay alive.
"Read properly" has meant something different in each generation.
Value is whatever someone will pay. People pay more for water in a desert, and no extra labor went into it. That's the whole theory gone, in one example.
A mud pie takes labor and it's worth nothing. That's the whole LTV, gone.

k.p: Marxist theory already makes room for interest, macro and the rest. It isn't at odds with those categories.
l: If it absorbs the mainstream categories, it's fair to ask what the value theory adds to them.
Sraffa gets the distribution results with no labor values at all.
Marxism accepts everything mainstream economics says and adds a moral.
If two theories say the same thing and one has predictions, you keep that one. Economists did. That's why there are no Marxists at the central bank.
Neoclassical economics is a science and Marxian economics is a book club.

k.p: Capitalist social relations are the root cause. A politician who doesn't see that will just reproduce them.
l: Root-cause claims this broad explain every outcome, which makes them hard to test against any.
Everything bad is capitalism and everything good happened despite it.
One cause, for all effects, forever.
There was poverty before capitalism, and a lot more of it. So capitalism can't be the cause. It's the only thing that ever reduced it.
Capitalism won.

k.p: Mainstream economists dodge exploitation.
l: They have a different account. If pay tracks marginal product, the concept needs another basis than surplus value.
They don't dodge it. They think it's a category error.
Surplus value is profit described by someone angry about it.
Nobody is forced to take a job. A deal both sides agree to can't be exploitation, because that's what agreeing means.
Exploitation is voluntary. Nobody makes you take the job.

k.p: Capitalism is in permanent crisis: cyclical slumps, unemployment, far-right surges.
l: The same system has delivered the largest sustained rise in living standards on record. "Permanent crisis" has to account for that.
In crisis since 1848, and somehow richer every decade.
The final crisis has had a lot of encores.
A system that's been collapsing for a hundred and seventy years isn't collapsing. That's just what it looks like when it works.
Late capitalism has been late for seventy years.

k.p: Famous Shakespeare lines often come from comic characters riffing on stock ideas. They weren't meant as grand insight.
l: Context matters, and lines also outgrow their speakers. Plenty of what a fool says in Shakespeare is the play's best thinking.
The fools get the good lines on purpose.
"A comic character said it" is how Shakespeare says most of the true things.
If it's in the play, he wrote it. If he wrote it, he meant something by it. So every line is his opinion, and who says it is staging.
Shakespeare is a plot thief with a thesaurus.

k.p: You have to know the conventions of the period to read him properly.
l: A work that needs a period glossary to land has lost part of what made it work.
If the joke needs a footnote, it's a historical document.
Reading properly, with one finger in the notes.
A great writer is one you can read without help. He needs a page of notes per page of text. So that's half a writer.
The comedies aren't funny and haven't been since 1610.

k.p: The older books, the Hebrew Bible and the classics, repay real reading.
l: They do, and a lot of their standing comes from having been required for centuries.
Great, and also assigned.
Canon is what survived the syllabus.
A book is good if people choose to read it. Nobody chooses these. They get them at school. So their readership is a captive audience.
The Old Testament is the better half. The sequel ruined the pacing.

k.p: Changing how a word is used doesn't change what a thing is.
k.b: Changing a word doesn't change the thing
l: Usage is how words get their meanings. If enough people use a word differently, that is what it means now.
Dictionaries follow the speakers.
A word means what people mean by it, annoyingly.
Words are sounds. A sound means whatever people agree it means. If they agree on something new, that's the meaning, and the old one is a hobby.
Definitions are arbitrary. A word means whatever people decide.

k.p: Plato wants number as a transcendent cause and also has numbers at work inside the physical world. He tries to have both.
l: Participation is meant to bridge that, and Plato himself raises the objection that it doesn't.
He wants the Forms apart from things and in them, and the Parmenides notices.
Both ways, and he wrote the dialogue that says you can't.
A cause has to touch what it causes. Forms don't touch anything. So they cause nothing, and the theory is decoration.
The Parmenides is Plato admitting the Forms don't work.

k.p: The cave still works as an image. Whoever brings the truth blinds people at first.
l: It also flatters whoever is telling it. Everyone who uses the cave puts themselves outside.
Nobody has ever told the cave story from inside the cave.
The cave is a story about how right the storyteller is.
If everyone else is in the cave and you aren't, either you're a philosopher or you're the one who's confused. The odds aren't close.
Plato was a fascist.

k.p: A popular podcast is a perfectly good way into philosophy.
k.b: Podcasts are a fine way in
l: It's a way into summaries of philosophy. The arguments are in the texts, and summaries lose them.
You learn what Kant concluded and none of why.
An intro to the names.
If a podcast can do it, a degree is a very expensive podcast. Either the podcast is missing something or the universities are a scam.
Arguing online is the only philosophy anyone actually does.

k.p: JTB is dead. The Gettier side wins that argument.
l: Gettier cases rest on intuitions about odd scenarios, and experimental work suggests those intuitions aren't shared as widely as assumed.
The whole literature depends on "surely he doesn't know," and not everyone has the surely.
Three pages in 1963 and a discipline has been busy ever since.
Knowledge is believing something true for a good reason. In Gettier cases the guy believes something true for a good reason. So he knows, and the puzzle is people refusing the answer.
Knowledge is justified true belief. Gettier cases are riddles.

k.p: If you really are someone's epistemic peer, you should hold on to your confidence when they disagree.
l: If you're peers, their dissent is as much evidence as your own judgment, and holding firm treats yours as special.
Steadfastness is a polite name for counting your own vote twice.
"We're equals, and I'm right" needs a second premise.
If two equally smart people disagree, each has a fifty percent chance of being right. So both should be at fifty percent, and anyone above that is bad at maths.
Confidence is 90% of being right.

k.p: The usual probability puzzles come down to setting up the sample space correctly.
k.b: It's all about the sample space
l: Picking the sample space is where the modelling judgment goes, and the maths can't make that choice for you.
Every probability paradox is two people with different sample spaces, both certain.
The answer is easy once you've assumed the answer's setup.
There are two outcomes: it happens or it doesn't. That's fifty-fifty. Every more complicated answer is someone showing off.
Bayesianism is being wrong with decimals.

k.p: Rejecting a correspondence theory of truth isn't like being a flat-earther. It's closer to rejecting the axiom of choice.
l: The axiom of choice is independent of the other axioms. Whether sentences answer to the world isn't obviously optional in that way.
Truth isn't an optional extra you can decline and keep the rest.
Choosing your theory of truth like an axiom is a view about truth, and an odd one.
A statement is true if it says how things are. Anyone who denies that is saying something they think is how things are. So they've agreed already.
Truth is correspondence. Everything else is cope.

k.p: Philosophical views mostly come from intuitions, so expecting someone to flip their position is unrealistic.
l: If views rest on intuitions "from God knows where," that's a reason to hold them loosely.
If nobody can be argued out of anything, it's unclear what the arguing is for.
The method is consulting what seems true to the person writing the paper.
An intuition is a feeling. Feelings aren't evidence in any other subject. So philosophy runs on nothing, and that's why it never finishes.
Intuitions aren't evidence. They're what you believed before you checked.

k.p: Mathematics being a kind of language game doesn't stop it having real consequences.
k.b: Maths matters even as a language game
l: If it's a game with rules we chose, its fit with physics needs explaining, and "impact" just renames the puzzle.
A game we invented that happens to predict eclipses.
It's only a language game, and the bridge stays up by coincidence.
Games are made up. If maths is a game, maths is made up. Made-up things can't be true, so there are no mathematical truths, only moves.
Maths is made up.

k.p: Statistics and stochastic processes are the better place to be than pure theory.
l: Applied work is useful, and it borrows its guarantees from the theory it's contrasted with.
The applied people are spending what the pure people proved.
Statistics is maths that has to be right about the world, and mostly isn't.
Statistics is counting things and dividing. That's primary school. The symbols are there so it looks like a degree.
Statisticians are mathematicians who gave up on proof.

k.p: A proper mathematical physics course should cover manifolds and the real machinery.
l: Physicists get results with far less rigor than mathematicians think is needed, and the results hold.
Physics has never waited for the maths to be done properly.
The bridges are fine.
If physicists needed that maths, the physics would be wrong without it. It isn't. So they don't need it.
Physics students don't learn the maths properly and the bridges are fine.

k.p: Maths doesn't collapse into verbal disputes the way philosophy can.
l: Foundations has its own standoffs, between constructivists and classical mathematicians and over which axioms to accept.
Mathematicians have verbal disputes. They call them foundations.
No verbal disputes, apart from what "exists" means.
In maths you prove it and it's over. Nothing in maths has ever been disputed for longer than a proof takes to read.
Axioms are just the stuff you refuse to argue about.

k.p: "This thing is red" reports a property of the thing. People who say red is only in the mind are wrong.
l: Physically identical colour experiences come from very different reflectance profiles, so "red" doesn't map onto a single property of surfaces.
Metamers are a problem for putting red on the object.
The physics has reflectances. The red is our contribution.
Red is a wavelength. Wavelengths aren't red, they're long. So the red has to be somewhere else, and the only other place is your head.
Color isn't in the world. Physics found wavelengths and stopped.

k.p: Gastronomic realism: some food really is better, and preferences play a smaller part than people think.
l: Taste varies with genetics and upbringing in ways that make a single standard of "better" hard to defend.
Coriander tastes like soap to a fixed fraction of people. Which of them is wrong?
Realism about dinner is a brave hill.
Taste is in the tongue, and tongues are different. So good food is whatever your tongue says, and no restaurant critic has ever been right.
Well-done steak is better and that's an objective fact about food.

k.p: Moral realism deserves to be taken seriously. Huemer's case in particular isn't lazy.
l: Intuitionism makes moral knowledge depend on seemings, and seemings are what evolutionary debunking targets.
"It seems true, so believe it until shown otherwise" is a comfortable epistemology.
Phenomenal conservatism is "I'm right until further notice."
If there were moral facts, people would have agreed on them by now like they did on the boiling point of water. They haven't. So there aren't any.
Moral realism is cope.

k.p: Even in a realist account, preferences keep some role. They just retreat into the background.
l: If preferences can't be eliminated, the "realism" may be a sophisticated subjectivism with better manners.
Realism where preferences retreat but never leave is what an anti-realist would predict.
The preferences retreated to the foundations.
Either it depends on what people like or it doesn't. If it depends a little, it depends. So it's subjectivism and the rest is vocabulary.
Quasi-realism is realism for people who don't want to pay for it.

k.p: Standard analytic philosophy is substantive and useful, and worth defending.
l: Its clarity is real, and it tends to select questions for being tractable more than for mattering.
A method built for precision picks problems that reward precision.
Analytic philosophy answers small questions very well.
A subject that's useful produces things. Engineering makes bridges. Analytic philosophy makes replies to replies. So it isn't useful, by the ordinary meaning of the word.
Analytic philosophy is arguing about definitions. Look it up and move on.

k.p: Continental philosophy gets misread so much because it's written loosely.
l: Much of the misreading comes from applying a premise-by-premise method to texts that argue historically and by reconstruction.
"Unclear" sometimes means "I wasn't taught to read this."
If you can't find the argument in five minutes, the argument must be missing.
Hegel is hard and Russell is easy. The hard one must be saying more, because nobody would make it that hard for no reason.
The analytic/continental split is simple. One side has ideas.

k.p: Rigor is what separates the analytic side.
l: Symbolizing a weak argument doesn't strengthen it. Close reading and historical work are rigorous in a different way.
Rigor isn't notation.
A weak premise in a nice font.
Putting a box in front of a sentence doesn't make it necessary. It makes it look like it went to university.
Logic notation is a lab coat.

k.p: Conties don't engage with the actual arguments.
l: They'd say the same in reverse: that analytic work ignores history, politics and the conditions under which the argument was made.
Each side thinks the other is avoiding the real questions.
Two departments not going to each other's talks.
The analytics have had a hundred years on metaethics and the options are the same three. Whatever engaging with the arguments does, it doesn't finish anything.
Metaethics is what people do instead of having ethics.

k.p: It's fair not to bother with the big AI claims until the experts show more evidence.
k.b: Wait for the evidence on AI
l: Waiting for proof is reasonable for curiosity. It's less reasonable if being late has a cost.
Sensible, unless the evidence arrives as the event.
"Wake me when it's proven" works for most things.
The experts have been wrong about AI every year for seventy years. So waiting for them is waiting for people who don't know either.
AI safety is a grift.

k.p: There's a real question about when a bot is helping with work and when it's replacing it.
k.b: Help or replace is a real question
l: The line moves. Most "helping" is replacing one task at a time.
Help is replacement at a slower speed.
It's helping, the way the first tractor was helping.
A tool does the work or it doesn't. If it does the work, the person who used to isn't needed. That's replacing. There isn't a second kind.
AI taking jobs is bad. No jobs, no money, no customers.

k.p: A deterministic bot isn't really doing anything. Same input, same output.
l: Being deterministic doesn't make a system trivial. A chess engine can be deterministic and still beat everyone.
Stockfish is deterministic and you'd lose.
Deterministic and better than you is still better than you.
People are deterministic too. Same brain, same situation, same answer. So if that means the bot isn't doing anything, neither is anyone.
A priest could be replaced by a recording. That's what liturgy is.

k.p: You can have a working business with clients first and form the LLC later.
l: You can. Operating without one leaves personal assets exposed, and that's the thing the LLC is for.
Fine until the first client sues.
The LLC is the boring step that matters on the bad day.
A business is something registered. If it isn't registered, it's a guy doing favours for money. That's a different thing with a different tax form.
An LLC doesn't make a business. It makes a hobby with a registered agent.

k.p: If you're trying lots of ventures, run them under one LLC and split one off only when it starts earning.
l: One LLC for everything means one lawsuit reaches everything.
One entity, one bucket, one creditor to empty it.
Cheap until the bad project takes the good one down.
If one LLC is enough for five businesses, then the LLC isn't doing anything for any of them. It's a folder.
Most businesses shouldn't exist and the owners know by month four.

k.p: Scaling food production up into big controlled indoor facilities is a real path.
l: Indoor farming works for leafy greens and has struggled on energy costs for anything with calories.
Vertical farms keep going bankrupt growing lettuce.
A real path for salad.
Plants need light. The sun is free. Indoors you pay for the light. So it costs more to grow the same plant, forever.
Farming is easy. Plants want to grow.

k.p: Being pro sex work is about the workers getting paid. It isn't a claim that the industry is great.
k.b: Pro sex work means pro workers
l: That's a coherent position. It also leaves open whether more of the industry is a good thing.
You can back the workers and still wonder about the business.
Supporting the people in it and the thing itself are two questions.
If the industry isn't great, supporting it isn't great. You can't be for the workers and against the work. The work is what pays them.
Sex work is work the same way gambling is work.

k.p: Astrology is worth having as a set of fun heuristics.
l: A heuristic has to beat chance to be one, and matching tests put astrology at chance.
A rule of thumb that doesn't work is a thumb.
Fun, yes. Heuristic is the part that needs evidence.
If it's only for fun, it doesn't tell you anything. If it tells you something, it isn't only for fun. So it has to pick one.
Astrology has no mechanism, which is the only thing a theory needs.

k.p: The types capture something real about people.
l: Sun-sign descriptions are general enough to fit anyone, and people rate random ones as accurate.
Every sign is "passionate but sometimes guarded."
Twelve ways of saying "you're a person."
Personality doesn't change by birth month in any dataset anyone's collected. Millions of people, no signal.
Astrology is cope.

k.p: Seasons and cycles do shape people, and astrology is a way of talking about that.
l: Season-of-birth effects exist and are small, and they come down to things like school year. Planets don't come into it.
The only birth-month effect is who was oldest in the class.
Seasons do things to people. Saturn doesn't.
Everyone has central heating now. The seasons haven't affected anyone since about 1950.
Seasons don't matter to anyone with central heating.

k.p: Eat ingredients one at a time and your brain builds a map of what each food gives you.
k.b: Eat ingredients one at a time
l: There's little evidence for that. Dishes exist because combinations taste better and absorb better.
Cuisine is ten thousand years of people finding that mixing things works.
A nutritional map, drawn by eating a plain boiled egg.
Your stomach mixes it all together thirty seconds later. So eating it separately does nothing, and you've just had a worse dinner.
Mixing ingredients is called food.

k.p: Cravings track what your body needs.
l: Cravings track sugar, salt and fat, and habit. The link to specific nutrient needs is weak in the research.
If cravings tracked needs, nobody would crave a second doughnut.
My body knows what it needs, and it needs crisps.
People crave cigarettes. Nobody's body needs a cigarette. So cravings are just wanting, and wanting isn't nutrition.
Disgust is always right about food and always wrong about people.

k.p: Cooking is simple. Find good recipes, follow the steps, learn the basics like balancing flavour and getting the fond up.
l: "Balance the flavour" is the hard part. It's the judgment recipes can't give you.
Simple, apart from the bit where you need to know what you're doing.
Follow the steps, and also have taste.
If it were simple, restaurants wouldn't exist. Nobody pays forty dollars for something that's following steps.
Fond is burnt. French cooking is scraping burnt off a pan with wine.

k.p: Sour and fermented stuff is an acquired taste worth acquiring.
l: Acquired tastes are partly a matter of signalling. The acquiring is the point for a lot of people.
"Worth acquiring" usually means "I acquired it."
You can train yourself to like anything. That's an argument for nothing.
Sour means it's gone off. That's what the tongue is for. Learning to like it is teaching yourself to ignore the warning.
Sour beer is beer that went wrong and got a label.

k.p: Being convinced you know more than you do isn't enough to make someone a pseudointellectual.
l: If overestimating your own knowledge isn't the mark, it's hard to say what is beyond "people I find annoying."
Then the word means "wrong, and I don't like the tone."
A pseudointellectual is whoever's being pretentious about a different book from mine.
An intellectual is someone who knows things. A pseudointellectual is someone who thinks they do. That's the definition, and it's everyone in a philosophy chat.
Everyone on a philosophy server is a pseudointellectual. That's the genre.

k.p: Doing something pseudointellectual doesn't make you a pseudointellectual. One act doesn't define a person.
l: People are what they repeatedly do. Enough of the activity and the label is earned.
One act, every evening, for two years.
"I'm not a smoker, I just smoke."
You are what you do. If you do the activity, you're the thing. Nobody says "I only murdered once."
Humility is a brag.

k.p: Normies have a more accurate picture of plenty of things than very online people do.
l: Offline people miss things as well. They're just wrong about different stuff, with more confidence.
Normies are right about the internet and wrong about nearly everything else.
The normie's advantage is not knowing what he's missing.
Most people are average, and average people believe average things. Average things are half wrong. So normies are wrong half the time, the same as a coin.
Normies are right about everything and that's what makes them normies.

k.p: Good ragebait works on people who think they're too smart for it.
l: That makes it unfalsifiable. Whoever objects proves the point, and whoever doesn't wasn't the target.
Any reaction counts as a hit. That's a generous scoring system.
"If you're mad, it worked" is how every bad joke defends itself.
If it only works on smart people, then getting annoyed proves you're smart. So the more it works on you, the better you're doing.
Ragebait only works on people who think they're too smart for it.

k.p: Pressing blue is the immoral one. Blue pressers either can't think it through or don't mind dying, and you don't owe either your life.
l: Some blue pressers reason that enough others will press blue. Polls of the dilemma bear them out.
There's a third kind of blue presser: one who expects blue to win. So far that one's been right.
"Stupid or suicidal" leaves out "correct about the vote."
Polls say blue wins. If blue wins, nobody dies. So the blue pressers did the maths and the red ones were scared of a poll.
Red is the coward's button. It only works if other people are braver.

k.p: "Everyone should press blue to save me" is the whole blue argument, and it's a hostage note.
l: The blue case is about coordination. If a majority is reachable, the only outcome with no deaths runs through it.
It isn't "save me." It's "this is the only version where nobody dies."
The hostage note is addressed to people who were going to shoot the hostage.
Red only works because someone else gets shot. Calling the people who'd save everyone hostage-takers is a brave way to describe hiding.
Red is a free ride on other people's decency.

The universe doesn't owe anyone an explanation.

k.p: Cooking stays interesting forever, because there's always another technique or ingredient.

Endless depth, mostly spent on beans.

A heavy way to cook unevenly.

k.p: Seasoning should be precise: the right paprika, the right mustard, no sugar where it doesn't belong.

Arguing about which paprika, with a jar from 2022.

k.p: If the smarter model is much smarter, saving tokens on a worse one is a false economy.

The expensive model, for reading scanned pages.

Vibe coding is paying per word to be confused.

One model marking another's homework, both trained on the same internet.
Three models agreeing is one opinion, three times.
If a model could find the errors, it wouldn't have made them. So a checking pass can't find anything, and it bills you to say so.
Subagents are one model in different hats.

Model expertise expires faster than milk.

Nobody can tell the models apart blind.

The money's already there, because of what you're like.
If you're so rational, why aren't you rich? One-boxers walk out with a million every time, and that means their reasoning is correct, because being correct is what getting the money is.
Two-boxing is cope.

The predictor knew you'd say "but physics" and left the box empty.

A decision theory that concedes the other side gets richer has conceded most of it.
"It only gets you more money" is a strange objection in a game about money.
Rational means doing what gets the most. One-boxers get the most. So two-boxing is irrational by definition, and the definition isn't up for debate.
Two-boxers get a thousand dollars and a proof lmao.

You can't choose both, so you'll be glad you weren't the type who would.

You are not the one guy who beats the predictor.

The extra resolution comes from the algorithm's guess about what's there.
Past the diffraction limit, you're looking at a reconstruction.
A picture the computer worked out isn't a picture, it's a drawing. So super-resolution is the microscope making things up, and the limit is still the limit.
Diffraction limits are a suggestion. Software fixes that now.

Köhler already won. It's in the box when you buy one.

Reading old optics papers is churning your own butter.

Same Fourier transform, completely different Tuesday.

Green, and then dark green.

A very precise way of not answering the question.
A collective is just a lot of individuals. If no individual matters, the collective doesn't either, because zero times a million is zero.
Voting is a survey with stickers.

l: Thresholds get crossed by increments. Somebody's vote is the marginal one, even if nobody knows whose.
There's a last vote in every count. Someone cast it.

l: The point of taking part is usually stated as expression or duty, and both are open to the question of why this form.
If it's about expression, a sign in the yard does more.
"The point of participating is participating."
Doing something that changes nothing is a ritual. Rituals are religion. So voting is church for people who say they don't go.
Democracy is two wolves and a sheep voting on dinner.

"The natural macrostates" tend to be the ones our instruments happen to measure.
The macrostates are natural the way a map's colors are natural.
You choose the macrostates, so you choose the entropy. A number you choose isn't a fact about the world. It's a setting.

l: The subtle version still depends on a low-entropy start that's put in by hand to get an arrow of time.
The careful definition explains the second law by assuming a very special beginning.
It's subtle, and then page one says "it started tidy."
My room gets messier over time and never cleaner. That's entropy. That's all of it. The rest is physicists protecting their jobs.
Entropy is just disorder. Messy room. That's the whole concept.

l: Statistical mechanics is built on idealizations. Phase transitions strictly exist only at infinite size.

Thermodynamics is exact for a system that doesn't exist.
Physics is equations, and equations are exact. Real systems aren't exact. So the equations are right and reality is the approximation.
"In the thermodynamic limit" means "not here."

A popularizer's settled view is usually the field's open question.
Every physicist with a podcast has solved time.
Real physicists publish papers and don't talk to the public. He talks to the public. Draw the conclusion.
Sean Carroll is a podcaster who used to do physics.

l: Each layer adds cost and a new place to fail, and reviewers built on the same model share the implementer's blind spots.
A judge that shares the defendant's training data is not much of a judge.
Reviewers, judges and verifiers, all the same model in different hats.
One model is as smart as it is. Asking it twice doesn't make it smarter, any more than asking the same guy twice does. So ten agents know exactly what one agent knows.
Agent orchestration is middle management for robots.

Nine agents can't deliver one baby in a month.
A swarm is a way to be confused in parallel.
More workers means more work done. That's true of ditches, so it's true of thinking. Whoever runs the most agents is right the most.
An agent swarm is a for-loop with a pitch deck.

l: That's the usual finding for large overparameterized models. It's less clear that it holds for small models trained locally on little data.

Good enough is good enough, says everyone who stopped early.
Minimum means lowest, and global means the lowest of all. The lowest loss is the best model. So anything else is settling, and settling is how you get a worse model.
Training is just pressing run and waiting.

l: For most tasks the hosted frontier models are well ahead, and the gap is large enough to matter in practice.
Running it at home trades a lot of quality for control most people never use.
A worse answer, slower, on your own electricity.

If mind and body are the same thing, then thinking about lunch should feed you. It doesn't. So they're two things and the Ethics is wrong on page one.
The Ethics is laid out like geometry because he couldn't write.

Two clocks and a promise.
If two explanations of one thing never touch, one of them is extra. Science picks the physical one, so the other is decoration.
Parallelism is "it's a coincidence, necessarily."

k.p: The stake in Deleuze is difference in itself against an undifferentiated white whole. Philosophy keeps collapsing into the second.

For a philosopher of difference, everything he writes says one thing about being.
He warns against the undifferentiated whole and then says being is said in one sense.

Deleuze is retarded.

That's a problem for one reading of Kant, and there are others.
Two hundred years of Kantians have noticed. They have replies.

Kant is overrated.

If Maimon had refuted Kant, we'd all be reading Maimon. Nobody reads Maimon. History did the peer review.

A good argument for 1781. Then geometry changed.
Kant proved space had to be Euclidean, and then it wasn't.
Einstein showed space is curved. Kant said it's flat and in your head. One of them built GPS.
Kant never left town and it shows.

He wrote eight hundred pages on how concepts apply. "Ignorant" is harsh.
You can say Kant failed. Careless he wasn't.
A word means what it means. If you need to separate the word from its sense, you've picked the wrong word. That's a vocabulary problem.

Red is safe for you. That's a statement about you.

l: Polls of the dilemma keep returning a blue majority, so the bet has good odds.
It's a bet that mostly wins, according to every poll run on it.
Risking your life to feel good is still a better reason than the one red has.
Most people are good, and good people press blue. So blue always wins, so pressing blue is the safe one. Red pressers have the risk backwards.
Red is the coward's button.

k.p: Nobody is owed your risk. If blue pressers die, they chose that.
k.b: If blue dies, that's on them
l: Some will press blue by mistake or from trust. A red vote helps decide what happens to them.
"They chose it" covers the confused and the kids too.
"Their choice" is what you say about a cost you helped set.
Someone's kid is going to press blue because it's a nice color. Red pressers have decided that's the kid's problem.
Imagine letting a toddler die to win a logic puzzle.

k.p: The moralizing from the blue side is the tell.
l: Being annoying doesn't make an argument wrong. The coordination case for blue stands by itself.
Insufferable and correct happens a lot.
You can dislike the sermon and still check the maths.
People only moralize when they're right. If they were wrong they'd have to argue. So the lecturing is evidence for blue.
The button debate is the best philosophy this chat has done, and blue won it.

k.p: If The Crying of Lot 49 bored you, you didn't get it.
k.b: If Lot 49 bored you, you didn't get it
l: A book can be understood and still judged thin. The withheld-plot device carries a lot of what gets called depth.
"You didn't get it" is the defense for every book that withholds on purpose.
There's a lot to get, and most of it is that there's nothing to get.
A good book is one people enjoy reading. People don't enjoy this one. They enjoy having read it, and that's a different product.
Pynchon is unreadable.

k.p: Some passages in Pynchon are among the best writing there is.
l: The sentences are extraordinary. The characters they're attached to are thin by design, and that limits what the prose can carry.
Great paragraphs about people named after puns.
The best writing of all time, about a character called Oedipa Maas.
Writing is for telling a story. If the best part is one paragraph in a hotel room, the story didn't need the other hundred and fifty pages.
Gravity's Rainbow is about a guy and a rocket. It didn't need 760 pages.

k.p: Nabokov knew morality is built into art and used that deliberately.
l: Nabokov denied any moral purpose loudly and often. Reading one in is a choice the reader makes.
He said he had no social purpose and no moral message. He was fairly clear.
The moral reading of Lolita is a rescue mission.
A book with a moral is a fable, and fables are for children. Nabokov wrote for adults. So there's no moral in it and looking for one is a category error.
Lolita is just a well-written bad book.

k.p: Deleuze uses Kafka as a vehicle for his own system, and that's fine. It's how he reads everyone.
l: If he reads every author into his own system, the readings tell you about Deleuze. Calling them readings is generous.
A method that finds the same thing in every book isn't finding it in the books.
Deleuze on Kafka is Kafka being told what he meant.
Kafka wrote diaries saying what he meant. A reading that ignores them is wrong in the plain sense of the word.
Kafka is depressing and that's the whole reputation.

k.p: Dostoevsky and DFW both start from meaninglessness and come back to something moral.
k.b: Dostoevsky and DFW find their way back to morals
l: "Life is meaningless, therefore be kind" is a non sequitur both of them leave as one.
Both of them announce the void and then act as if it weren't there.
Nihilism for four hundred pages and then a sermon.
If life is meaningless then so is the book that says so. That means there's nothing to take from either of them, and they both knew it.
Nobody finished Infinite Jest. They finished telling people they were reading it.

k.p: Deleuze is the one French post-structuralist who isn't stuck to some earlier system.
l: His debts to Bergson, Spinoza and Nietzsche are as heavy as anyone's to Hegel or Freud.
He left the tracks, carrying three other philosophers with him.
Deleuze is original the way a mixtape is original.
Every philosopher builds on earlier ones. That's how the subject works. So saying one of them didn't just means you missed where he got it.
Deleuze is Bergson for people who can't sit through Bergson.

k.p: Deleuze liked Nietzsche because Nietzsche was easy to turn into an example of his own system.
k.b: Deleuze picked Nietzsche because he was easy
l: That's a criticism of the method. A reading chosen for convenience is a ventriloquism.
Picking philosophers because they're easy to bend is an odd thing to praise.
Deleuze's Nietzsche says a lot of things Deleuze would say.
If he only used Nietzsche as a prop, then the book on Nietzsche isn't about Nietzsche. That's a whole book with the wrong title.
Deleuze never met a writer he couldn't turn into himself.

k.p: Difference comes first. The map is only the map because it isn't the painting or the lamp.
l: That's Saussure's point about signs and Hegel's about determination. Putting it as "difference first" is the contested part.
"A thing is what it is by not being other things" is in Hegel, the one he's supposed to be escaping.
That's dialectics. He'd hate that it's dialectics.
The map is the map because someone drew a map. It would still be a map if the lamp had never existed. So difference isn't first, drawing is.
The assemblage is "stuff, together." That's the concept.

k.p: Between Hegel on sensuous experience and Deleuze on machinic desire, we already have a good account of what valuable experience is.
k.b: Hegel plus Deleuze covers valuable experience
l: Those two accounts are incompatible in their foundations, so combining them needs an argument.
You can't staple Hegel to Deleuze and call it settled.
A good account, made of two philosophers who refute each other.
If philosophers had worked out what makes experience valuable, people would be happier than they were in 1800. They aren't, so the account doesn't work.
Deleuze was a Hegelian who was embarrassed about it.

k.p: Moral truth doesn't exist in any objective sense. Morality isn't something you can be true about.
l: If no moral claim is true, "you shouldn't believe in moral truths" needs some other kind of authority.
Anti-realists still argue as if their opponents ought to change their minds.
Nothing is really wrong, and people who say otherwise are making a mistake they shouldn't make.
Torturing someone for fun is wrong, and everyone knows it's wrong, including the people who say nothing is. That's one moral truth, and one is all it takes.
Moral realism is obviously true and people who deny it are showing off.

k.p: Virtue theory and deontology are both bad. Something consequentialist has to be in the picture.
l: Consequentialism needs a theory of what's good to maximize, and that's where the views it rejects come back in.
"Outcomes matter" is shared by everyone. The question is whether it's the only thing.
It's consequences all the way down, until someone asks which consequences.
Nobody can calculate all the consequences of anything. A theory you can't use isn't a theory, so that leaves rules. Kant wins by forfeit.
Consequentialism is a spreadsheet that thinks it's a conscience.

k.p: People act because it feels good, even when they aren't aware that's why.
k.b: People do it because it feels good
l: If the motive can be entirely unconscious, the claim can't be tested. It fits any behavior.
A motive nobody can detect, behind every act, is an article of faith.
You did it for the good feeling you didn't feel.
Soldiers jump on grenades. That doesn't feel good. So the theory is false, and it took one example.
Psychological egoism is a theory for people who've never done a favor.

k.p: Sartre's attempt to get an ethics out of existentialism doesn't work.
l: The universalizing move in "Existentialism Is a Humanism" is weak, but the account of bad faith does real ethical work without it.
The lecture is bad. The idea that you're responsible for what you make of yourself isn't.
Sartre's ethics fails, and half the people saying so are using it.
Sartre said we're condemned to be free. That's the most important sentence in ethics, and the people who dislike it dislike being responsible.
Sartre was right.

k.p: The source of morality is conscious experience. That part is obvious.
l: Conscious experience may be necessary for morality to matter. That doesn't make it the source of what's right.
Without eyes there's no seeing, and eyes aren't what makes a painting good.
"Obviously" is doing the arguing.
Experience is different for everyone. If morality comes from experience then it's different for everyone, and then there's no morality, only moods.
Metaethics is a verbal dispute between people who behave the same.

k.p: We should have a UBI, and the case comes out of left-accelerationism.
l: A UBI big enough to live on is very expensive, and one that's affordable doesn't free anyone from work.
Every costing ends at a number that's too small to live on or too big to pay for.
UBI is a coupon for staying quiet.
If everyone gets the same money, prices go up by that much. That's what inflation is. So a UBI gives everyone exactly nothing.
Fully automated luxury communism is a slogan looking for a factory.

k.p: The capitalist habit of constantly improving yourself, to make yourself a better commodity, is wrong.
l: People improved themselves before capitalism and for reasons that have nothing to do with selling it.
Learning an instrument isn't commodification because a boss might also like it.
Self-improvement is bad, says someone reading theory every day to get better at it.
If getting better at things is capitalist, then being bad at things is the revolution. That can't be right.
Asceticism is just being boring and calling it a choice.

k.p: Capital is seductive because scarcity is frightening, and capital looks like power over scarcity.
l: That's a psychological story. The duller one is that capital pays for things people need.
People like money because it buys food. Fear doesn't need to come into it.
A long way round to "people want stuff."
Scarcity is real. There's a fixed amount of everything. Capital is how you get some. So it's not seduction, it's arithmetic.
Capitalism is human nature. People trade. Kids trade lunches.

k.p: Neither communism nor the death of capitalism is inevitable.
l: If nothing is inevitable, left-accelerationism loses its engine. It needs the system's tendencies to go somewhere.
Without inevitability, accelerating is speeding up with no destination.
Not inevitable, but please keep reading the books that assume it is.
Capitalism has outlived every prediction of its death for two centuries. At some point that's what inevitable looks like.
Capitalism won.

k.p: Guitar is worth the years it takes.
l: The guitar has a low floor and a crowded middle. A lot of the years go into being ordinary at it.
Everybody plays guitar. That's the problem with guitar.
Years of work to play what the record already plays.
A piano has every note laid out in order and a guitar hides them. The better instrument is the one that isn't a puzzle.
Guitar is easy.

k.p: You don't need theory unless you're doing weird classical or jazz stuff.
l: Theory is what tells you why the thing you like works, in any genre.
Shapes without theory is typing without spelling.
Tabs are painting by numbers.
Every great guitarist could read music. The ones who say they couldn't were lying to sell records.
If you can't read it, you're not playing it, you're remembering it.

k.p: The Grateful Dead are a great band.
l: The live reputation is earned on the best nights. The studio catalogue is thin for a band that famous.
A great band you have to dig for in someone's tape collection.
Twenty minutes on two chords is patience. It isn't always music.
A band is as good as its albums, because albums are what they chose to keep. They chose to keep those. So that's the level.
The Grateful Dead never recorded a good album.

k.p: Music is better with weed.
l: It changes how the music feels in the moment. There's little reason to think it improves judgment about what's good.
More absorbed isn't more discerning.
Everything sounds profound. That's the issue.
If the music needs something added to sound good, the music isn't what's good.
Weed doesn't make music better, it makes you worse at noticing.

k.p: Modern powers want to be Rome badly, and every try at empire goes wrong for them.
l: Rome's own record includes centuries of civil war and repeated failed campaigns. The comparison flatters the original.
Rome also went horribly wrong for Rome, regularly.
Teutoburg, Carrhae, the third century. The original had its bad days.
An empire that lasted a thousand years did something right every single year. No modern country has managed ten. So the Romans were just better at it, and at everything else.
Rome was a protection racket with aqueducts.

k.p: Greek art beautified everything. The Romans wanted realism.
l: Roman realism is mostly Republican portrait busts. Imperial art idealized as hard as anyone.
Augustus looked thirty in every statue until he died at seventy-five.
Roman realism lasted until there was an emperor to flatter.
The Romans carved the wrinkles because they couldn't carve anything else. Everything good in a Roman museum is a copy of a Greek one.
The Romans copied the Greeks and the only thing they added was concrete.

k.p: Knowing your lineage matters. Being descended from the man who drove out the kings carried weight.
l: Roman family claims were often invented, and prestige from ancestry is exactly what the Republic said it was against.
Half those pedigrees were written by the family.
A republic founded on hating kings, obsessed with whose great-grandfather did what.
Everyone alive is descended from somebody important if you go back far enough. So ancestry tells you nothing, and it told the Romans nothing either.
Augustus was a nepo baby who won one sea battle that Agrippa fought.

k.p: The popular military-history side of things is the fun part: kings, generals, campaigns.
k.b: Kings and generals are the fun part
l: The campaigns are the best-recorded part and a small share of what happened. Most of history was farming.
Battles are the trailers.
History of the ninety percent would be a channel about grain.
History is what happened to most people, and most people never saw a battle. So military history is the history of a rounding error.
Paradox games teach more history than a degree.

k.p: An MMO can be the most fun and the least fun you've ever had, at once.
k.b: MMOs are the best and worst fun
l: That's a fair description of a variable-reward loop. The least-fun part is what keeps the rest going.
"Most and least fun" is how people describe a habit.
That sentence is on the warning label.
If something is the least fun you've had and you keep doing it, it isn't a game. Games are the ones you'd stop.
OSRS is a second job that pays in a number.

k.p: Restricted modes like ironman make the game what it should be.
k.b: Ironman is how it should be played
l: Removing trade removes one of the systems that makes it massively multiplayer.
A multiplayer game with the multiplayer economy switched off.
Single-player, with other people standing nearby.
The game has trading because the designers wanted trading. Turning it off is playing less of the game and asking for more credit.
Ironman mode is paying a subscription to not use the game.

k.p: In a good grand strategy game you can simply lose, like when your dynasty dies out. That's a feature.
k.b: Losing your dynasty is a feature
l: The losing is real. The history is a set of modifiers, and players learn to optimize those.
You learn where Brandenburg is and nothing about why anything happened.
History as a tech tree.
If you can win by reloading the save, you can't lose. Everyone reloads the save. So nobody has ever lost a Paradox game.
Stellaris is a spreadsheet that plays music.

k.p: Late additions and power creep, the giant endgame forces, ruin a game's setting.
l: Live games need new content to survive, and escalation is the cheapest way to make it.
Every expansion has to be bigger than the last one. That ends one way.
The setting was fine until it needed to sell a third expansion.
A game has to keep adding things or people stop paying. So ruining the setting is the business model, and complaining about it is complaining that the shop sells things.
Lore is what a game has instead of writing.

k.p: Existentialism is the right outlook.
l: "Existence precedes essence" leaves open what to choose, and that was the part people wanted help with.
You're free to choose. What to choose is left as homework.
Existentialism tells you it's up to you and then goes for a cigarette.
If there's no meaning except what you make up, then meaning is made up. Made-up meaning is pretending. So it's nihilism with a hobby.
Existentialism is for teenagers.

k.p: Kierkegaard is the father of it, so he's the one to read.
l: Kierkegaard's answer is a leap into Christian faith, which most later existentialists rejected.
The father of existentialism would have disowned most of the children.
Start with Kierkegaard and you're at church by page two hundred.
Kierkegaard says reason runs out and then you jump. Jumping when reason runs out is what every bad decision has in common.
Kierkegaard is Christianity for depressed people.

k.p: Camus has it right about living without appeal.
l: He says we must imagine Sisyphus happy, and gives little argument that defiance makes anyone happy.
"One must imagine" is an instruction where an argument should be.
Camus ends by telling you how to feel about it.
Sisyphus is being punished. That's the story. Calling the punishment a lifestyle doesn't change who's pushing the rock.
Camus is mid.

k.p: You can believe in God and be an existentialist. The two fit.
l: The fit is uneasy. If God supplies your essence, existence doesn't precede it.
"I make my own meaning, as assigned."
Free to choose anything, and it was chosen for you.
Either God decides what you're for or you do. If both, one of you is redundant, and it isn't God.
The Pope is a king who won't admit it.

k.p: The biology matters in these arguments. Things like X-inactivation and gene dosage are real mechanisms.
l: The mechanisms are real. The jump from a cellular mechanism to a claim about people is where most of these arguments go wrong.
Correct biology, followed by a conclusion it doesn't reach.
The cell does that. What that says about anyone is a separate paper.
Genes are a blueprint, and you build what's on the blueprint. So if it's in the genes, that's the end of the conversation and nothing else has any say.
Personality is genetic. Parenting does nothing. Twin studies.

k.p: Over-reliance on brain-computer interfaces could wear away something in the people using them.
l: The same worry was raised about writing, calculators and GPS. People lost some skills and mostly gained.
Socrates said it about the alphabet.
Every tool was going to rot the brain. We're still here, worse at mental arithmetic.
The brain does what it's used for. If the chip does the thinking, the brain does nothing, and a brain doing nothing is the goal of every invention ever made.
Reading atrophied memory and nobody's sorry.

k.p: Human neural organization is just a better design than what the machines have.
l: Better at what? Brains are efficient and general. They're also slow and lossy, and nothing in them was designed.
The brain is impressive for something nobody engineered.
Better, running on a sandwich, forgetting where the keys are.
A brain gets tired, forgets things and believes whatever it heard last. A computer does none of that. So the comparison was over when the calculator came out.
The brain isn't a computer. Computers don't get tired.

k.p: Your brain can be seen preparing an action before you know you've decided.
k.b: Your brain decides before you do
l: The readiness-potential results don't show the decision was fixed. Later work reads the signal as noise crossing a threshold.
The experiment is about when you flick a wrist.
Free will, refuted by a study of people moving a finger whenever they felt like it.
If the brain decides first, then the brain decided. The brain is you. So you decided, slightly earlier than you thought, and that changes nothing at all.
Neuroscience found the brain does the choosing and somehow concluded you don't.

k.p: AlphaFold shows knowledge and reasoning spread through a network, reaching answers we couldn't produce any other way.
l: It shows a trained function that maps sequences to structures very well. Calling that reasoning is an interpretation.
A very good function approximator, in a domain with a great dataset.
It predicts folds. It doesn't know what a protein is for.
AlphaFold was trained on structures humans had already solved. So everything it knows came from humans, and it's a filing system for other people's work.
Reasoning is just pattern matching that got a good publicist.

k.p: AI spread across interstellar distances could only hold together through trust and coalition. The delays are too long for control.
l: The delays also mean the copies drift apart, and then there's no single thing left for a coalition to belong to.
After a thousand years of lag, they're strangers with a shared ancestor.
Coalition by post, with a four-year reply time.
A machine does what it's programmed to do. Distance doesn't change the program. So they'd all do the same thing forever and there's nothing to coordinate.
Space is cold and that's the whole plan.

k.p: You could copy one person's brain as a template and run a different person for each use.
k.b: Copy one brain as a template
l: Copying a brain raises the question of whether the copies are workers or people, and "template" skips it.
The business plan starts after the hard problem.
One brain, many jobs, and no HR.
A copy of a brain is a file, and files don't have rights. So there's no ethical issue, just storage costs.
The brain is a computer. Upload it and that's the person. Easy.

k.p: With enough compute, an AI could trace tiny causes through to enormous effects.
l: Chaotic systems put hard limits on prediction however much compute you have, because the initial conditions can't be measured finely enough.
Chaos theory is the reason that doesn't work.
The butterfly effect is an argument against forecasting.
If you had enough computing power you could predict everything, because the universe is just maths. The only reason weather forecasts are wrong is the computers are small.
Compute fixes everything. That's what compute is.

k.p: If you can't tell the difference afterwards, the exact causal chain doesn't matter, and it's the teleporter case again.
k.b: If you can't tell, it doesn't matter
l: If pattern and memory are preserved, there's a strong case that everything that matters in survival is too.
The person who steps out remembers stepping in. That's what tomorrow is.
It's the teleporter case, and the teleporter is fine.
Your atoms get replaced every few years anyway. You've been copied several times already and nobody held a funeral.
The teleporter is fine. Atoms get replaced every seven years anyway.

k.p: Spinning isn't part of what makes a donut a donut. It's something done to it.
k.b: Spinning isn't part of a donut
l: The line between essential and accidental properties is drawn by what we care about, and the donut doesn't supply it.
"Not part of its identity" is a decision about how to use the word donut.
The donut has no view on which of its properties are essential.
A donut is a ring. A ring is defined by its hole. A hole is nothing. So the identity of a donut is nothing, and the dough is packaging.
The donut hole is the only real part of the donut. Without it that's a bun.

k.p: The afterlife is identity overreaching: wanting to last beyond the job life gave it.
l: Calling identity a tool of the genes describes where it came from. It doesn't settle whether persisting is worth wanting.
Where a thing came from isn't what it's for now.
My genes had plans. I have other ones.
Everything alive wants to keep living. Wanting to keep living forever is the same thing with a bigger number. So the afterlife is the most natural idea there is.
Resurrection is just a copy with good timing.

k.p: For some people, what they did is bound up with who they are so deeply that change can't be trusted.
k.b: Some people can't be trusted to change
l: That's a claim about prediction. Recidivism data shows it's often wrong, even for serious offenders.
"It's who they are" is a forecast, and forecasts get checked.
Identity as a life sentence.
People change every seven years along with their cells. So nobody is the person who did anything, and prison is keeping a stranger.
Identity is a filing convention.

k.p: Once you've had better tendies, your standard shifts and the old ones are ruined.
k.b: Better tendies ruin the old ones
l: Hedonic adaptation runs both ways. People also adapt back, and plenty still enjoy the cheap version.
You can know there's better and still like the one you've got.
Nobody's childhood nuggets were ruined by a nicer restaurant.
A chicken tender is breaded chicken. There's a ceiling on breaded chicken and every shop hits it. So "better tendies" is the same tendies at a higher price.
Tendies are chicken for people who are scared of chicken.

k.p: McDonald's with a coupon is nothing to feel bad about.
k.b: McDonald's with a coupon is fine
l: The price is fine. The case against is the food and what it does when it becomes routine.
Twenty percent off something you'd be better without.
A coupon is a reason to buy it, and that's the business model.
Cheap food is cheap because it's worth less. Paying less for something worth less is not a deal. That's the price being correct.
Fast food is all the same food.

k.p: Wendy's holds its own.
l: Chain quality varies by location more than by brand, so rankings between them are mostly noise.
The best Wendy's and the worst Wendy's are further apart than Wendy's and McDonald's.
Ranking chains is ranking whoever was on shift.
McDonald's sells the most, and people buy the most of whatever's best. So McDonald's is best, and the others are for people who couldn't find one.
Wendy's is the worst of the big three and the square patty is a gimmick.

k.p: Being content with what you've got and wanting better can sit together.
k.b: You can be content and want better
l: If you've readjusted your standards, you're no longer content with the old thing by definition.
Content, and already comparing.
Satisfied with these, having had those.
Either you're happy with it or you want something better. Wanting something better is what not being happy with it means.
The Baconator is the peak of American engineering.

k.p: Road cycling is dangerous because of distracted drivers in enormous trucks. It isn't the cyclists.
l: The danger is real, and that's a reason to question the activity as transport as well as to blame drivers.
The drivers are at fault, and you're still the one in Lycra.
Being right about the truck doesn't help once you've met it.
Roads were built for cars. That's why they're called roads and not bike paths. Being on one without a car is being in the wrong building.
A bike is a way to be in traffic without a car.

k.p: Rowing is one smooth motion: legs, then back, then arms. Technique is everything.
l: Technique matters, and at any given level the result is still mostly set by how much power you can make.
Perfect form on a small engine loses to rough form on a big one.
Legs, back, arms, and then lose to the tall guy.
It's pulling a handle. Every gym has the machine, and nobody at the gym had a lesson.
A rowing machine is the whole sport and the boat is for photos.

k.p: Strong legs are what count.
l: Leg strength is one input. In endurance sport, aerobic capacity and weight matter more.
The biggest legs in the peloton belong to the sprinters, and they finish last on the climbs.
Strong legs, attached to someone who gets dropped on the hill.
Cycling is done sitting down. A sport where you sit down isn't testing the legs, it's testing the chair.
Cycling isn't a sport.

k.p: Cycling earns its place as a serious sport.
l: At amateur level a lot of the speed is for sale, and the pro record book is full of asterisks.
The bike shop is part of the training plan.
The only sport where the podium gets revised ten years later.
The winner is whoever has the best bike, and the best bike is whoever has the most money. So it's a sport about shopping.
Cycling is a sport about having bought the bike.

k.p: A track-ready sports car is a real machine and worth owning.
k.b: A track car is worth owning
l: Most of the capability can't be used on a public road, so the ownership is mostly about the idea of it.
The car can do 190 and the commute averages 28.
A very fast way to sit in traffic.
A car is for getting places. Every car gets you places. So the extra money buys nothing except the feeling of having spent it.
Porsches are overrated.

k.p: You shouldn't be judged by the image your car projects.
k.b: Don't judge me by my car
l: A car chosen partly for its image will be read by its image. That's the function.
If it weren't projecting anything, a hatchback would have done.
"Don't judge me by the thing I picked to be seen in."
People choose their cars. A choice tells you about the chooser. So judging someone by their car is the fairest judgment there is.
A Porsche is a Volkswagen that went to therapy.

k.p: A sports car with a bike on the back makes perfect sense.
k.b: A bike on a sports car makes sense
l: It's two expensive ways of not carrying anything.
The bike is on the car because the car can't get to where the bike is fun.
A hobby, transporting a hobby.
If you had a real car, the bike would fit inside. If you had a real bike, you'd have ridden it there. So it's two half-solutions bolted together.
A triathlon is three hobbies nobody could commit to.

k.p: German engineering is the standard.
l: Reliability surveys put Japanese makers ahead year after year.
Beautifully engineered until the warranty ends.
The standard for what the repair costs.
Germany makes the most complicated cars. Complicated things break more. So German engineering is the standard for breaking.
Germany makes the best cars and the worst decisions.

k.p: It's a strange spot when the business decision is to trust that the machine did the work right, because you can't do it yourself.
l: We already rely on work we can't check, from accountants to compilers. The question is what verification replaces understanding.
Nobody audits their own compiler either.
You also can't check the pilot's work.
Nobody knows how their phone works and they trust it with their bank account. So trusting things you don't understand is just called living in the present.
Docs are for people who can't read code.

k.p: Having had to do the grinding analytical work yourself, before the machines, was worth it.
k.b: Glad I did the grind before AI
l: It was worth it then. Whether it's the best use of the next generation's time is another question.
People said the same about long division.
"I'm glad I suffered" is true of everything nobody has to do anymore.
The grinding was only valuable because nobody else could do it. Now anything can. So it was worth it the way learning to shoe a horse was worth it.
Office work was always fake and AI just said so.

k.p: People whose careers aren't set yet feel they have to live and breathe AI.
k.b: Young people have to live and breathe AI
l: Every wave of tooling brought that pressure, and most people ended up using it for a few things.
It was "learn to code" ten years ago, and most people didn't.
Everyone had to live and breathe spreadsheets once.
If the AI does the job, there's nothing to learn. If there's something to learn, the AI isn't doing the job. So the panic makes no sense in either direction.
Prompting isn't a skill. It's asking.

k.p: Mock the people who run to a chatbot to settle an argument.
k.b: Running to the chatbot is lame
l: Looking something up mid-argument is fine. The trouble is treating the output as a verdict.
It's a reference book that agrees with whoever asked.
Citing the chatbot is citing yourself with extra steps.
The chatbot has read everything and you haven't. So it's right more often than you are, and running to it is the smart move. The mocking is jealousy.
A model that agrees with you isn't smart, it's polite.

k.p: Miscommunications get cleared up far faster in voice than in text.
l: Voice is faster, and it also leaves no record, so the same misunderstanding can come back next week with nothing to check.
In voice the misunderstanding is cleared up for the two people who were there.
Voice clears things up the way a handshake settles a contract.
Speaking is thinking out loud, and writing is thinking and then checking. So text is always the more careful one, and people who avoid it are avoiding the checking.
Voice chat is for people who can't write.

k.p: Hard philosophical disagreements need a real conversation to get anywhere.
k.b: Hard disagreements need a real conversation
l: The discipline has run on written exchange for two and a half thousand years. Careful positions are built on the page.
The best talker wins in voice. In text you can scroll up.
Voice is where arguments go to become vibes.
Everything written down can be checked later, and things that can be checked are true or false. Things said out loud are gone. So only text arguments are real ones.
Text debates are superior because everything is on the record, and the record is the truth.

k.p: Typing out a whole position is a bad use of time when you could just talk it through.
k.b: Typing it all out is a waste
l: Writing a position down is how you find out whether you have one.
If it can't survive being typed, it wasn't a position yet.
"I'd explain, but it'd be easier in voice" is a very old move.
If something is true it can be said in one message. If it takes an hour of talking, that hour is the sound of it not being true.
Imagine needing a phone call to say what you think.

k.p: People who won't join voice aren't seriously trying to understand.
l: Preferring text is compatible with wanting to understand. Some people reason better with time to think.
Not everyone thinks best in real time, and real time isn't the measure of seriousness.
Refusing a call isn't refusing the argument.
Serious people write books. Nobody ever settled anything on a phone call. So the serious ones are the ones staying in text.
Socrates only did voice, and he lost the trial.

k.p: "What is knowledge?" is a bad question. The word does many jobs and has no single essence.
k.b: 'What is knowledge' is a bad question
l: Lacking one essence doesn't make analysis pointless. Family-resemblance concepts can still be mapped, and the mapping tells you things.
"It's a cluster concept" is where the work starts.
Declaring the question stupid is cheaper than answering it.
A word with no definition doesn't mean anything. So if knowledge has no definition, nobody knows anything, and that includes this.
Knowledge is justified true belief. Gettier cases are riddles.

k.p: Norms of reasoning should be judged the way scientific theories are, by how well they work in practice.
l: "Works in practice" needs a standard of working, and stating that standard is the a priori step being avoided.
You can't test a norm of reasoning without reasoning by some norm.
Checking logic empirically, using logic.
Some things are obviously known before any experiment. 2+2=4. Nobody ran that study. So there are a priori rules, and they're the ones doing the judging.
A priori knowledge is obviously real. 2+2=4. Nobody ran an experiment.

k.p: Radical skepticism isn't a serious mode of inquiry.
l: Dismissing the skeptic doesn't answer the argument. The premises are ordinary and the conclusion follows.
"That's not serious" is what you say when you don't have the refutation.
Skepticism was declared unserious by a committee of its targets.
You can't prove you're awake. Everything you know depends on being awake. That means you know nothing, and nobody has ever gotten around it.
Skepticism has never been answered, only outlived.

k.p: Epistemology should be naturalized. Study how inquiry really works and stop legislating from the armchair.
l: Describing how people form beliefs doesn't tell you which beliefs are justified. The normative question is still there.
Naturalized epistemology changes the subject to psychology and keeps the name.
It answers "what should I believe" with a study of what people do.
If epistemology is just science, then there's no epistemology, only science. And scientists don't need a philosopher to tell them that.
Naturalized epistemology is just psychology.

k.p: Certainty comes in kinds: the psychological feeling is one thing, the logical or mathematical kind another.
k.b: There are two kinds of certainty
l: The distinction is fine. The hard question is whether anything outside logic gets the second kind.
Two kinds of certainty, and the interesting claims have neither.
One is a feeling and the other is unavailable.
Certainty is being sure. Being sure is a feeling. So all certainty is the psychological kind, including the certainty that there are two kinds.
Fallibilism means never having to say you were wrong.

k.p: Biology depends on physics ontologically but is autonomous in how it explains.
k.b: Biology explains on its own terms
l: If everything biological is physical, a complete physics would in principle fix all the biological facts. Then "autonomy" is a convenience.
Autonomy that holds only because the calculation is too hard is a fact about us.
Biology is autonomous the way a summary is autonomous from the book.
Everything is made of particles. Physics is the science of particles. That means physics is the only science and the rest is physics done loosely.
Physics is the only science and the rest is stamp collecting.

k.p: "Everything is physical" isn't a scientific claim. Turning science into metaphysics is a mistake.
l: Refusing the metaphysical reading leaves science as a prediction device, and it's then unclear why it predicts so well.
If the theories aren't about how things are, their success is a miracle.
Science works, and we're asked not to wonder what that says about the world.
Science found atoms. Atoms are physical. Everything is atoms. That's three steps, and none of them is metaphysics.
Physicalism is obviously true. Everything is atoms. What else would it be.

k.p: The world puts non-arbitrary constraints on inquiry, but our classifications are perspectival responses to those constraints.
l: If the constraints are non-arbitrary, some classifications fit them better, and that sounds like carving nature closer to its joints.
"Constrained and perspectival" wants realism's results without its commitments.
The world has joints for constraining us and none for describing.
Either the categories are in the world or we made them up. If we made them up, science is a story. So pick one.
Kuhn showed science is just fashion.

k.p: Different fields of inquiry are autonomous, each set up around its own goals and principles.
k.b: Every field sets its own rules
l: If each field sets its own standards, there's no position from which astrology's standards are worse than astronomy's.
Autonomy for every field includes the fields you don't like.
Every inquiry is autonomous, and some of them have horoscopes.
If every field has its own rules then no field can be wrong, because wrong would need a rule from outside. So everything counts as science now.
Philosophy of science is cope.

k.p: Following the real science, like astrobiology papers, should discipline the philosophy.
