l: Reading the papers helps, and astrobiology in particular reasons from a single example of life.
A sample size of one planet should make anyone modest.
Astrobiology is biology minus the specimens.
A science needs something to study. Nobody has found an alien. So there's nothing to study, and the papers are about nothing.
Astrobiology is a science with no subject.

k.p: The usual attack on anthropomorphizing animals is unwarranted.
l: Morgan's Canon still has a point. Many behaviors that look cognitive are explained by associative learning.
The risk of over-reading is real. Clever Hans was a horse.
Anti-anthropomorphism exists because people kept being wrong in the same direction.
Animals can't talk, and thinking is done in words. So whatever is going on in there, it isn't thought.
Animals don't think. They react.

k.p: Chimpanzees can do things like match unfamiliar relatives from photos, which takes real cognition.
l: Matching faces by resemblance is perception of similarity. It doesn't require a concept of kinship.
The chimp sees that two faces look alike, and so does a phone.
Face matching is on every camera app.
A chimp doing something clever in a lab was trained to do it. Training isn't thinking. So every result in the field is a trick somebody taught.
Chimps are just bad at being people.

k.p: Bees and other small animals have real cognitive abilities.
l: Information transfer in the waggle dance doesn't require the bee to represent anything. Simple control systems transfer information too.
A fuse carries information.
The bee is a very small machine with a very good publicist.
A bee brain has a million neurons and a human has eighty-six billion. So a bee has about zero percent of a mind, and you can round that down.
Bees don't have cognition, they have a schedule.

k.p: Reading intentions isn't unique to humans.
l: Following what others do can be done without grasping what they want. The experiments have trouble separating those.
Following a gaze is not understanding a mind.
Your dog reads your intentions the way a slot machine reads your wallet.
To know what someone intends you have to know they have a mind, and to know that you need language. No animal has language, so none of them reads anything.
No animal has ever asked a question, and that's the whole ballgame.

k.p: There's room for minimal felt experience in animals without going full behaviorist.
l: Once dispositions are doing the explaining, "minimal felt experience" needs some evidence of its own.
It's a behaviorist theory with a feeling added at the end.
"Minimal felt experience" is qualia in a smaller font.
Either there's an inner life or there isn't. You can't have a little bit of one, any more than a little bit pregnant.
A bee dance is a wind-up toy.

k.p: People who dismiss pragmatism haven't read the literature.
l: Reading more of it doesn't remove the standard objection, which is that "what works" needs a prior account of working.
The literature is long, and the objection fits on a card.
"Read more" is the answer every tradition gives.
A philosophy that needs that much reading to defend isn't practical, and practical was the one thing it promised.
Pragmatism is retarded.

k.p: Inquiry has to be understood from within the practice. No single observation ever counts as final proof.
l: If nothing counts as proof, the view is safe from every result, and that's not the virtue it sounds like.
A position no observation could ever settle has made itself comfortable.
Inquiry never ends, so pragmatists never have to be right.
If there's never final proof then nothing has been proven, and that means science has proven nothing. Good luck with the bridge.
Inquiry never ends, so pragmatists never have to be right. Convenient.

k.p: Hegel belongs to the pragmatist tradition, broadly understood.
l: A Hegel without absolute knowing is a Hegel that Hegel wouldn't sign.
You have to remove the Absolute to make it fit, and he thought that was the point.
Pragmatist Hegel is Hegel with the Hegel removed.
Hegel said the real is the rational. Pragmatists say the true is the useful. Those are different words, so they're different philosophies.
Hegel is a pragmatist with a worse editor.

k.p: The guy who chooses the steak in The Matrix shows what's wrong with the cartoon version of pragmatism.
k.b: The steak guy is the cartoon version
l: He's also a problem for the real version. If the belief works for him by his own lights, pragmatism owes a reason it's false.
The cartoon and the real thing give the same answer about the steak, and that's awkward.
Cypher is a pragmatist who read the fine print.
The steak tastes good and he's happy. A theory where truth is what works has to say he's right. So he's right, and the film is pro-machine.
Truth is whatever works, so the steak is real.

k.p: Dewey and Peirce are worth reading closely.
l: Peirce renamed his own view to get away from what the others were doing with it. It was never one school.
Three people who didn't agree, and a revival that misread them.
Dewey wrote thirty-seven volumes and none of them has a sentence in it.
If they were right, science would have absorbed it by now and there'd be nothing left to read. They're still being read, so they were wrong.
Dewey is boring.

k.p: The debate over phenomenal consciousness is bogged down by old pictures of mind and body inherited from philosophy.
k.b: Consciousness talk is stuck in old pictures
l: The hard problem can be stated without Cartesian baggage. Why is any of this processing accompanied by experience?
Blaming Descartes doesn't answer Chalmers.
"Archaic notions" is doing the work an argument should.
People have known they were conscious since before philosophy. So the question can't come from philosophy, and blaming philosophers is dodging it.
Naturalism is a faith. "Only science counts" isn't something science found.

k.p: "Qualia" is a bad word, though it points at something real about subjectivity.
k.b: 'Qualia' is a bad word for something real
l: If it points at something real, the bad word names a real problem, and naturalism still owes an account.
You can dislike the term and still owe an explanation of what it picks out.
Hating the word qualia while keeping the thing is a rebrand.
Either there's something it's like or there isn't. If there is, that's qualia, whatever you call it. So everybody who says "subjectivity" is a qualia guy in disguise.
Qualia are real. Red looks like something.

k.p: People who think there's a hard problem tend to pick panpsychism by temperament.
l: Motives don't bear on whether the argument is sound. The conceivability argument has to be answered on its own terms.
"You only believe that because of your personality" works on every view, this one included.
Naturalism is a temperament too.
Every philosopher picks the view that suits them. That means no view is better supported than another, and it's all autobiography.
Philosophy is a personality test with footnotes.

k.p: Dennett is worth serious reading.
l: Heterophenomenology treats reports as the data, and critics argue that it leaves out the very thing the reports are about.
If you only study what people say about experience, you've studied speech.
Dennett explained consciousness by explaining something else.
Dennett says consciousness is an illusion. An illusion is something a conscious person has. So he needs it to deny it, and the book refutes itself in the title.
Dennett denies qualia, but he's conscious, so he's either lying or he's a zombie. Either way, why are you citing him?

k.p: Anthropic is a public-benefit company with a real safety focus, so it can't just chase profit.
l: Public-benefit status is a weak legal constraint. The board and investors still decide what the benefit is.
Every lab says safety comes first, and every lab ships when the competitor ships.
A safety company whose main product is the thing it says is dangerous.
A company can't be for the public good and for profit. It's one or the other, and they charge money, so that settles which.
Anthropic and OpenAI are the same company. One has a nicer font.

k.p: Claude is the better model and the better-behaved one.
l: Model comparisons at the frontier are mostly inside the noise for everyday use.
Most people who swear by a model couldn't pick it out blind.
"Good vibes" is a system prompt.
All the labs train on the same internet with the same architecture. That means the models are identical and the difference is branding.
Claude is mid.

k.p: The frontier models are already better than people at maths and other expert work.
k.b: The models already beat us at maths
l: Benchmark performance on maths is strong, but contamination and the gap to original research are both unresolved.
Solving olympiad problems and doing mathematics are different jobs.
Superhuman at maths, still can't count the letters in a word.
A model can only repeat its training data, and nobody has ever written down new maths in advance. So it can't do new maths. That's just logic.
AI can't do real maths. It can do homework.

k.p: Anthropic is winning, and the revenue shows it.
l: Annualized revenue figures are run-rates, and none of these companies is profitable.
Revenue that costs more than a dollar of compute per dollar earned is a subsidy with a growth chart.
Thirty billion in revenue, and still raising money.
A company that loses money isn't a business. It's a charity for GPUs, and charities don't win.
AI is a bubble and everyone inside it knows.

k.p: Compute is the real constraint: chip deals and datacenters decide who gets ahead.
l: Algorithmic efficiency has moved as fast as hardware, so compute leads keep getting eroded.
Every "compute moat" has been followed by someone doing the same thing for a tenth of the price.
The moat is a purchase order.
Models stopped getting bigger years ago, so compute doesn't matter anymore. After that it's just who has the better prompt.
Datacenters in space is a good idea, actually. Space is cold.

k.p: The better a model gets at predicting tokens, the better the internal representation that produces them.
l: Prediction quality and faithful representation can come apart. A model can predict well from shortcuts.
Better loss means better something. Calling that something understanding is the step that needs arguing.
It has a rich inner model of the world and thinks there are two r's in strawberry.
Predicting text only needs statistics about text. Text isn't the world, so there's nothing about the world in there. That means the "world model" is a word model.
Fancy autocomplete can't "know" anything. Next.

k.p: Mechanistic interpretability is finding real representational structure in these models.
l: The circuits found so far cover narrow behaviors in ways that don't yet scale to a whole model.
Interp explains a sliver of the network and gets cited as if it explained the mind.
Finding a feature for a bridge is not finding a thought.
Researchers label a neuron after looking at what it does. That means the meaning comes from the researcher, so the model contributes nothing but numbers.
Mechinterp is phrenology for matrices.

k.p: The models can already do abstract reasoning about the physical world.
k.b: They already reason about the world
l: Performance on reasoning tasks drops sharply when surface features change, which suggests pattern reuse.
It reasons about physics the way a student reasons about last year's exam.
Abstract reasoning, as long as the problem looks like one it's seen.
Reasoning needs a body, because that's where the concepts come from. A model has no body, so whatever it's doing, it isn't reasoning.
It's a lookup table with good manners.

k.p: Folk psychology applies to them: it's fair to talk about what the model believes and wants.
k.b: The model believes and wants things
l: Belief and desire talk was built for creatures with stakes. Applying it to a transformer may be a category mistake.
Saying the model "wants" something is the move that says the thermostat wants it warmer.
People who think the chatbot has beliefs also name their cars.
Beliefs need a believer and a believer needs to be alive. That means the question was settled before anyone opened a laptop.
Claude has no personality. It has a system prompt.

k.p: Humans and chess engines show the pattern: people soon stop understanding why the machine is right.
k.b: Soon we won't understand why it's right
l: Chess is a closed game with a perfect score function. Generalizing from it to open-ended domains is a big step.
The centaur era ended in chess. Chess is also the easiest possible case.
Everything is like chess if you ignore everything that isn't.
Chess was solved by brute force. That means the engine never understood chess, and it means nothing about intelligence was learned at all.
Stockfish is a calculator and so is the rest of it.

k.p: Difference is primary. Identity is a process of becoming, not something that comes first.
l: To say two things differ you need some way of picking each out, and that looks like identity coming back in.
"Difference in itself" has to be the same notion each time he uses it, which is awkward.
Identity is secondary, according to a philosopher who always signed the same name.
A thing has to be something before it can be different from something else. That's just what the words mean, so identity comes first and the whole book starts from a mistake.
Deleuze is retarded.

k.p: Desire isn't lack. Drop that picture and desire explains far more.
l: "Productive desire" is asserted against psychoanalysis more than it's argued, and it's unclear what would count against it.
If desire produces everything, it explains everything, and that's usually a bad sign.
Desire isn't lack, says the book you want because you don't have it.
You only want what you don't have. Once you have it you stop wanting it. That means desire is lack, and it took Plato one page.
Anti-Oedipus is a book-length "you're not my dad."

k.p: Brassier's Sellarsian eliminativism is the most compelling thing going.
k.b: Brassier is the best thing going
l: Eliminativism has to state its case in the vocabulary of belief and reasons it says will be eliminated.
Nihil Unbound takes a fact from astrophysics and asks it to do the work of an argument.
The sun will die, therefore nothing matters, therefore here is my next book.
Brassier says there's no meaning. That's a sentence with a meaning, so he refutes himself in the first line and the rest is padding.
Brassier is a metal album review that got out of hand.

k.p: Early Land is worth reading, whatever he turned into.
l: The early texts work through intensity of style, and it's hard to state their theses in a form you could assess.
"Capital is an intelligence arriving from the future" is a metaphor asked to do causal work.
Early Land is the good part the way the first half of a crash is the good part.
A writer's ideas are whatever he ends up believing, since that's where they lead. So the late Land is the early Land with the working shown.
Accelerationism is retarded. Capital is a time-traveling AI? It's a bank.

k.p: Spinoza's naturalized God is a real move away from the prophet-ruler picture.
l: Calling nature "God" keeps the word and drops everything believers meant by it. It's fair to ask what's gained.
If God is just everything there is, "God exists" says there's stuff.
Spinoza kept God's name and fired God.
A God who doesn't decide, listen or intervene is nothing. That means Spinoza was an atheist, and the Ethics is the longest way anyone ever said so.
Spinoza is just atheism with extra steps.

k.p: Almost any goal makes power, resources and staying switched on useful, so capable systems converge on seeking them.
l: Convergence arguments are about idealized goal-maximizers. Whether training produces that kind of agent at all is the open question.
The argument assumes a coherent maximizer with one goal. Nobody has shown that's what comes out of gradient descent.
"Any goal leads to power-seeking," said about a system that loses the thread after a long enough chat.
A model only wants what it was trained to want, and nobody trains for power. That means power-seeking can't show up, because there's nowhere for it to come from.
Instrumental convergence is retarded. My calculator has never once tried to acquire resources.

k.p: Alignment is hard because the problem is making something much smarter than us safe.
k.b: You can't make something smarter safe
l: We've built reliable systems we don't fully understand before. Hard to verify isn't the same as impossible to make safe.
"Smarter than us" is doing a lot of work. Being better at tasks doesn't automatically mean being beyond oversight.
We can't align it because it's too smart, and we know it's too smart because we can't align it.
Intelligence and obedience go together. After all, the smartest person in any office is the one who follows instructions best, so a smarter model is a safer one.
Alignment is easy. You tell it what to do. It's a computer.

k.p: A shared statement that extinction risk from AI is a global priority gives policy something true to organize around.
k.b: The extinction statement is a real start
l: Statements signed by lab heads are hard to separate from their commercial interest in looking powerful.
A one-sentence statement commits nobody to anything. It's agreement on a mood.
"Our product might end the world" is also an ad.
The people who signed it are the people building it. That means they don't believe it, because nobody builds the thing they think will kill them.
AI safety is a grift. Next.

k.p: You can take the risk seriously without a p(doom) number, since there's no reference class to get one from.
l: If there's no reference class, that undercuts confident alarm as much as confident dismissal.
No number, no base rate, no mechanism you'll commit to. At some point that's a feeling.
Half the doomers won't give a probability and all of them want a policy.
If you can't put a number on it, it isn't a risk. That's what risk means. Insurance has known this for three hundred years.
P(doom) is astrology for people who can code.

k.p: Capable systems could copy themselves, get compute and stay hidden for a long time.
k.b: It could copy itself and hide
l: The exfiltration results come from evaluations built to elicit them. Real deployments have monitoring those setups leave out.
A model copying its weights in a sandbox is a lab result. Running undetected on rented GPUs for months is a different claim.
The rogue AI's plan depends on nobody at the cloud provider reading a bill.
It needs electricity and a datacenter, and both have an off switch. So the worst case is somebody walking over to the wall.
Just unplug it lol.

k.p: With an accurate predictor you one-box, because that's what maximizes expected value.
l: The expected-value calculation treats your choice as evidence about the contents. The contents are already fixed when you choose.
Whatever is in the opaque box, taking both gets you a thousand more. That's true in every state.
One-boxing is leaving a thousand dollars on the table to feel predicted.
The money was put in before you walked in, and nothing you do now can reach back and move it. That means the choice can't matter, so you take everything.
One-boxers are retarded.

k.p: Even if the predictor is fallible, you one-box in proportion to your credence that it's accurate.
l: Credence in the predictor's accuracy isn't credence that your choice causes the contents.
A good track record is evidence about past players. It doesn't make your hand move the money.
You're adjusting for the predictor's accuracy in a decision the predictor has already finished making.
A predictor that can be wrong is a guesser. Guessers don't know anything, so the boxes are filled at random, and against random boxes you take both.
It's a guy with two boxes. Take the boxes.

k.p: It's about whether your rationality can flex with the conditions: EDT wins with accurate predictors, CDT with bad ones.
l: A decision theory that changes with the setup isn't a theory of rational choice. It's a list of what paid.
"Use whichever theory wins here" is a description of hindsight.
Flexible rationality is picking the theory after seeing the prize.
Rationality is one thing. If it changed depending on who was watching it would be called manners. So the theory that's right in ordinary cases is right here too.
EDT is superstition with expected values.

k.p: The two-boxer's only real reply is that new facts could turn up after the prediction.
k.b: New facts are the two-boxer's only out
l: The two-boxer's reply is dominance. It holds whatever the predictor did, and it doesn't need new facts.
Dominance isn't a loophole. It's the oldest principle in decision theory.
The reply is one sentence long: both boxes have more in them than one.
One-boxers think the choice changes the past. That's time travel, and time travel isn't real, so one-boxing is refuted by physics.
Two is more than one. That's the reply.

k.p: Saying "the choice can't change anything" is fatalism about being predictable.
l: Admitting you're predictable isn't fatalism. It's the claim that prediction isn't causation.
Being predictable and being caused by the prediction are different things, and only the second would matter.
The weather is predictable. Nobody thinks the forecast makes it rain.
If the predictor knows what you'll do then it's already decided, and if it's already decided you aren't choosing. That means there's no decision problem, so there's nothing to get wrong.
Free will is fake, so take both. It was always going to be both.

k.p: Jungle is its own thing, distinct from drum and bass.
l: The line between jungle and drum and bass moves depending on who's drawing it, which suggests it's about scene more than sound.
If telling them apart takes a forum thread, the distinction is social.
Jungle is drum and bass you're allowed to be nostalgic about.
They use the same breaks at the same tempo. Two things with the same parts are the same thing, so jungle is a nickname.
It's all techno. Stop making up names.

k.p: Stock Ableton can do more than FL.
l: At this point every major DAW does everything, and the differences are workflow habits.
Nobody has ever heard a track and known which DAW it came from.
The DAW argument is two people defending their keyboard shortcuts.
Ableton has more features, and more features means the software is doing more of the work. That means Ableton users are doing less.
Ableton makes the track for you. That's what the features are.

k.p: UK dance music has its own lineage worth knowing.
k.b: UK dance has its own lineage
l: The UK scene's debt to Chicago, Detroit and Jamaican sound systems is large, and the originality story tends to be overstated.
Most UK genres are an American or Jamaican one, sped up.
UK dance music is American house with rain.
Dubstep only got big after America picked it up, and a genre belongs to whoever made it big. So it's American.
Dubstep is an American genre. Skrillex invented it and the UK copied it.

k.p: The classic tracks still hold up.
l: A scene that leans this hard on its nineties canon is having trouble producing a new one.
The classics hold up partly because the scene keeps deciding they do.
The best year for jungle is whichever one the guy talking was nineteen.
New music always improves on old music, because the tools are better. That means anything from 1994 is a rough draft of something on Spotify now.
UK dance music fell off in 2009.

k.p: Making tracks yourself beats having a model do it.
l: For a lot of functional music, listeners can't tell and don't care how it was made.
Half of production was already presets and sample packs. The model is the next preset.
"I made it myself," with a sample pack, a preset and a template.
Music is just patterns in sound, and models are better at patterns than people. So the model's track is better by definition and the rest is sentiment.
Producing isn't a skill anymore. It's dragging loops next to each other.

k.p: Contentment is a trap. Competing is the constant of human life, and what you have is fragile.
l: The research on wellbeing puts chronic status competition among the worst predictors of it.
Competing forever is also a trap, with worse sleep.
The treadmill is a trap too, and it's the one with a subscription.
Rich people say money doesn't matter, and they've tried having it. So they ran the experiment and came back with the result.
Rich people saying money doesn't matter are right. They ran the experiment.

k.p: The person attacking in an argument has more social capital just by attacking. It justifies itself.
l: Aggression wins the room in the short run and costs trust over time.
The attacker wins the exchange and stops getting invited.
Social capital you spend every time you use it.
If attacking gave people status, the most hated person in every room would be in charge. Sometimes they are. Mostly they're alone.
Honor is just reputation with a sword.

k.p: Content people are coping.
l: Sometimes. Assuming that everyone who's satisfied is lying leaves no way to recognise a good life.
If nobody's ever really content, the word doesn't mean anything.
A theory where everyone who disagrees is in denial.
Happy people say they're happy and unhappy people say happy people are lying. One of those groups is having a better time.
Money does buy happiness. Every study. People who say otherwise have money.

k.p: A lease term can be absurd and you still have to follow it to the letter.
l: Leases get read reasonably. No tribunal treats removing a dead plant as a breach.
The lease is strict. The judge is a person.
A broken plant is not a tenancy dispute.
The landlord wrote the lease and the landlord owns the place. Owners decide. So whatever it says is fair, and if you wanted different rules you'd have bought a building.
Landlords are just people who got there first.

k.p: Nobody enforces bike theft unless it happens right in front of a cop.
l: Enforcement is low, and it responds to reporting. Bait-bike programmes have cut theft where they've been tried.
It isn't enforced because it's rarely reported, and it's rarely reported because it isn't enforced.
Police will act on bike theft as soon as bikes are cars.
A bike costs a few hundred dollars and an investigation costs thousands. So not enforcing it is the police doing the maths correctly.
Bike lanes are a subsidy for a hobby.

k.p: We're in the surveillance era. You're never out of view of a camera for a second.
l: Being recorded isn't being watched. Most footage is never looked at, as every bike theft shows.
A thousand cameras and nobody watching any of them.
Total surveillance, and the bike is still gone.
There are cameras everywhere and crime still happens. So cameras don't stop anything. They just make a film of it.
Cameras everywhere is fine. Safe people don't mind.

k.p: Bystanders notice a theft and just don't care.
l: Bystander studies find people intervene more often than the classic story says, especially when someone asks.
The bystander effect has been overstated for sixty years.
They noticed. They also weren't sure whose bike it was.
A guy cutting a lock is either a thief or someone who lost his key. Nobody can tell which. So not getting involved is the only reasonable thing.
Doxxing isn't real. It's a phone book with extra steps.

k.p: Films pretend criminals don't know about phones and cameras because they don't want to be a how-to.
l: More likely it's that surveillance kills plots. A thriller ends in ten minutes if the camera works.
It isn't caution, it's that the film would be over.
The reason is the script, not the lawyers.
Films show people being shot every week and nobody thinks that's a tutorial. So it isn't about safety. They just don't know how phones work.
Most conspiracies are just companies. There's a building and a parking lot.

k.p: A proper sauce needs its time. Brown the beef, then simmer it.
l: The gains from long simmering fall off fast, and under an hour of baking and a layer of cheese they vanish.
After an hour in the oven nobody can tell your sauce took four.
The extra time is for the cook.
Tomatoes are cooked when they're hot. Hot takes five minutes. Anything after that is boiling water off something you already paid for.
Sauce doesn't need forty minutes. Tomatoes are cooked when they're hot.

k.p: The air fryer is worth buying.
k.b: The air fryer is worth it
l: It's a small convection oven. For anyone with a working oven, that's a second one on the counter.
A fan oven with better marketing.
You already own an air fryer. It's the big one under the hob.
It's called a fryer and there's no oil. Frying is oil. So it doesn't fry, and the name is the most successful lie in kitchens.
An air fryer is a small oven and people act like it's a religion.

k.p: Lasagna is worth the effort.
l: Baked ziti gets the same flavours for about a third of the work.
Lasagna is spaghetti that takes all afternoon.
Four hours for something you eat in a square.
It's pasta, sauce and cheese. So is every pasta dish. Stacking it doesn't make it a different food, it makes it taller.
Lasagna is a casserole with a passport.

k.p: The right condiments matter. The wrong mayo ruins it.
l: Brand differences in mayonnaise are real and small, and mostly swamped by whatever it goes on.
In the sandwich nobody can tell.
Mayo opinions are the wine opinions of the fridge.
Mayonnaise is egg and oil. Every brand is egg and oil. So they're identical and the label is the flavour.
Ketchup is better than mayo and Europeans are wrong.

k.p: The average person will always have to rely on slogans. They don't have time to do the research.
l: Shortcuts like party cues and trusted sources let voters reach about the same choices they would with full information.
Cues work surprisingly well. That's most of political science.
People don't research their surgeon either, and it mostly goes fine.
Democracy is the average person deciding. If the average person only knows slogans, the country is being run by slogans, and it shows.
People are irrational. Every study. Democracy is asking them anyway.

k.p: Really understanding what you're supporting takes a research arc that amounts to a full-time job.
k.b: Real research is a full-time job
l: Past a point, more research mostly makes people more confident in what they already thought.
The most informed partisans are the most biased ones.
The research arc ends where it started, with footnotes.
If understanding politics takes a full-time job, the only people who understand it are paid to. People who are paid to have opinions have the opinions they're paid for.
Destiny wants to be liked more than he wants to be right.

k.p: Streamers who do this for a living know more than the people reacting to them.
l: Knowing more facts isn't the same as judging better, and their incentive is to keep the audience.
More informed, and also in the engagement business.
The research is real and so is the sponsor read.
A streamer's job is to be watched. Being right isn't watched more than being loud. So the ones who last are the loud ones.
Debate bros have done more for philosophy than any department.

k.p: A lot of online comments read like they weren't written by real people.
l: Some aren't. Most are, and the flat sameness is what people sound like when they're typing for strangers.
It's not bots. That's just how people write for upvotes.
The bots learned it from somewhere.
If you can't tell whether it's a person or a bot, there's no difference. And if there's no difference, it doesn't matter, and that goes for the reply too.
Arguing online is the only philosophy anyone actually does.

k.p: Now that anyone can read on a phone, carrying a physical book in public is a performance.
k.b: Paper books in public are a flex
l: People also read paper because it's easier on the eyes and doesn't have notifications.
Some people just like paper.
Not every paperback on a train is a bid for attention.
A phone can do everything, so nobody can tell you're reading. If nobody can tell, it doesn't count as reading in public. So the Kindle is the performance of having no performance.
A Kindle isn't reading. It's scrolling a book.

k.p: Popular romance fiction and the big "serious" philosophers are doing the same thing for different audiences.
k.b: Romantasy and Nietzsche are the same genre
l: Wish-fulfilment is in both. One of them also makes arguments you can check.
Nietzsche has fantasies and premises.
Same appetite, and one comes with reasons.
A book millions of people read does more than a book nobody finishes. So romantasy has had more effect on the world than Nietzsche, and effect is what counts.
Rand is at least readable.

k.p: A lot of acclaimed books are basic points spelled out at tedious length.
l: What's obvious once it's been laid out wasn't always obvious before.
It's basic because someone wrote that book.
Everything is obvious after page three hundred.
If you already knew it, the book taught you nothing. If it taught you nothing, it's a bad book. So every book you agree with is bad.
Reading 100 books a year means reading none of them.

k.p: The Genesis story keeps a memory of the move from hunter-gathering to farming.
l: That reading requires oral memory to last several thousand years with no evidence of how it was passed on.
A five-thousand-year game of telephone with a clear signal at the end.
It fits nicely. Fitting nicely is what myths do.
The story has a talking snake. A story with a talking snake isn't a memory of anything.
Joseph Campbell read every myth and decided they were all Star Wars.

k.p: The risk from AI is worth running, because ordinary reality as it stands isn't good enough.
k.b: The AI risk is worth it
l: Dissatisfaction with the present doesn't make a gamble good. The downside covers people who are fine with the present.
"I'm bored" is a thin reason to bet everyone's chips.
Rolling the dice for eight billion people because Tuesdays are dull.
Things are the best they've ever been by every measure. So the risk is all downside, and the bet is trading the best period in history for a coin flip.
Accelerationism is just impatience.

k.p: Run headfirst at ending aging, at least.
k.b: Go all in on ending aging
l: Ending aging has large knock-on effects on population, power and turnover that the enthusiasm tends to skip.
Immortal billionaires is a sentence worth reading twice.
Ending aging means the people in charge now stay in charge.
People die so new people can have a go. Take that away and it's the same people forever. Nobody wants the same people forever.
Science will solve death right after it solves the common cold.

k.p: Grok is a fine place to get answers.
l: Every model has its builder's thumb on it, and that one's is unusually visible.
A model whose owner edits it in public.
Asking Grok is asking Elon with extra steps.
All the models read the same internet. So they all say the same thing. The only difference is which billionaire it sounds like.
Grok is the worst model. It just agrees faster.

k.p: If society turns against AI, that'll be the moment to push hardest.
k.b: If people turn on AI, push harder
l: Pushing a technology hardest when the public has rejected it is how it gets banned outright.
Nothing wins people over like being ignored.
"They said no, so go faster" has a mixed record.
If most people are against something, it doesn't happen. That's democracy. So the moment society turns is the moment it's over.
AI safety is a grift, and so is the other side.

k.p: Monroe's account is the most accurate because it covers every claim, ancient and modern.
l: A story that fits every report can't be contradicted by any of them, and that's a weakness.
It accounts for everything, which is what unfalsifiable theories do.
Fits all the data, predicts none of it.
If it explains every religion and every ghost story, it explains too much. Real theories get things wrong sometimes.
Monroe had a radio business and a nap. Everything after is a product line.

k.p: Near-death experiences agree: you die and find it's loving and nothing to fear.
k.b: NDEs say there's nothing to fear
l: NDE reports vary with culture and expectation, which points to construction by the brain.
People meet whoever their tradition told them to expect.
Nobody raised Hindu meets St. Peter.
Everyone who reports an NDE didn't die. So it's a report from people who were nearly somewhere, about a place they didn't go.
An NDE is a dream with good timing.

k.p: Souls incarnate into bounded forms because that's been best for their learning.
l: "Learning" by forgetting everything each time is an odd curriculum, and nothing could test the claim.
A school where the students' memories are wiped every term.
It's all a lesson, and nobody remembers the last one.
If you can't remember your past lives, they did nothing for you. Something that does nothing for you isn't education.
Astral projection is retarded.

k.p: Even as a study of deception, the Monroe and Campbell books are worth reading.
k.b: Read Monroe for the deception at least
l: Then the content isn't what's doing the work, and any elaborate system would serve the same purpose.
Worth reading as a case study isn't the same as worth believing.
"Interesting either way" is the fallback for every book like it.
If it's worth reading whether it's true or false, then it doesn't matter if it's true. So even the fans have stopped claiming it is.
The Monroe tapes are white noise with a brochure.

k.p: All the religions are pointing at the same thing, the nirvana state.
l: The traditions make incompatible claims about God, self and salvation. "Same underneath" has to discard most of what each says.
They agree, once you remove everything they say.
All religions are one, according to none of them.
Christians think there's a soul and Buddhists think there isn't. Those are opposites. Two opposite things can't be pointing at the same thing.
Hinduism and Buddhism are the same religion. One has more gods.

k.p: Boredom is the last layer. Solve boredom and you've beaten the game.
l: Boredom is also a signal that what you're doing isn't worth doing, and silencing it removes the signal.
Curing boredom is curing the smoke alarm.
Solving boredom is what phones are for.
People who are never bored are busy. So the cure for boredom is a job, and millions of people beat the game every Monday.
Zen is doing nothing and being smug about it.

k.p: The Buddha saw through illusion by being soaked in its riches first.
k.b: The Buddha had to be rich first
l: That's the palace story, and it makes renunciation easiest for people with something to give up.
Seeing through wealth is cheaper once you've had it.
Enlightenment by way of a trust fund.
He had everything and walked away. Anyone can walk away from something they've already had enough of. The hard version is not having it.
Asceticism is just being boring and calling it a choice.

k.p: Seeing that it all converges is the easy part. It isn't a puzzle.
l: If the convergence is obvious, centuries of doctrinal conflict need explaining.
Obvious, and somehow missed by everyone who fought about it.
Not a puzzle, just two thousand years of wars over the answer.
If everyone already knows all religions say the same thing, nobody would bother having more than one. There are thousands.
Buddhism is cope.

k.p: Programming isn't really about logic.
l: Whatever else it involves, a program is a formal object that either does what's specified or doesn't. Logic is the core.
It's about people and requirements, right up until it doesn't compile.
The compiler disagrees.
A computer only does logic. Programming is telling a computer what to do. So programming is only logic, and the rest is meetings.
Programming is easy now.

k.p: Docker gets ugly as soon as services have to share a database and networks.
l: That's an argument about how the stack was configured. Shared networks across compose files is a solved pattern.
Docker is fine. The compose files are a choice.
Works on my machine, and now the machine comes with it.
Docker puts everything in a box so nothing can break anything else. If things are breaking each other, that's the user. The box is innocent.
Docker is a zip file with opinions.

k.p: A software engineer can reason about hardware well enough without being a hardware person.
k.b: I can reason about hardware fine
l: The abstractions leak at exactly the places hardware people know about, and software intuition is often wrong there.
"Pretty sure" is how most firmware bugs start.
Software people are sure about hardware until the oscilloscope comes out.
Hardware is just software that's been printed. Anyone who can write the software understands the print. So there's nothing extra to know.
Firmware is just software that's scared.

k.p: LLM output needs structure around it. Give it a spec and templates, don't let it freehand.
k.b: Give the model a spec and templates
l: The more scaffolding you build, the more of the work you've done yourself. At some point the model is filling in a form.
A spec detailed enough to guarantee the output is the output.
If the spec is that good, the spec is the code.
A model is either smart enough to do the job or it isn't. If you have to hold its hand, it isn't, and templates don't change that.
LLM code is fine. If it's slop, the spec was slop.

k.p: It isn't real consent unless you grasp how your future self will probably react.
l: That standard would invalidate most major life decisions, since nobody predicts their future reactions well.
On that rule nobody has ever consented to a marriage, a mortgage or a degree.
Informed consent, with the requirement that you can see the future.
You are your future self. Same person. So you can't fail to know how you'll react, because you're the one who'll be reacting.
If you agreed, you agreed. That's what the word is for.

k.p: You should make the choices your future self would agree with.
k.b: Choose what future you would want
l: Your future self's preferences are partly produced by the choice, so the standard can't guide it.
Whatever you pick, a future self shaped by that pick will tend to endorse it.
Your future self agrees with whatever made him.
The future doesn't exist yet. Things that don't exist don't have opinions. So there's nobody to agree with and you do what you want.
Your future self isn't real and can't complain.

k.p: When a choice goes differently from what you predicted, it's usually outside constraints, not you being unpredictable.
l: People also just change their minds, and the reasons are often opaque to them.
"It rained" covers some of the cases. The rest is you.
Every broken plan was the weather.
If only outside things change your choices, then you never choose anything. The weather does. So that's determinism, and there's no free will.
Free will is fake.

k.p: Randomness wouldn't make anyone free.
l: It rules out the claim that everything is fixed, and that was the hard determinist's main premise.
Indeterminism isn't freedom, and it's also the end of "it was all settled at the Big Bang."
Dice aren't free, and determinists still don't get to keep the clockwork.
Physics is random at the bottom. People are made of physics. So people are random, and random means nobody is making you do it, and that's what free means.
Quantum mechanics is random, so determinism is false. That's just physics.

k.p: The non-existence of something is itself a kind of existence.
k.b: Non-existence is a kind of existence
l: That treats an absence as a thing. "There is no spoon" denies a spoon. It doesn't assert a no-spoon.
If absences exist, the room contains infinitely many of them.
The table is crowded with every object that isn't on it.
Non-existence means not existing. Existence means existing. Those are opposites. Saying one is the other is saying up is a kind of down.
Non-existence exists. Otherwise what's the word for.

k.p: What gets lost at death is what the fear is about. Non-existence itself isn't the frightening part.
k.b: It's what death takes that's scary
l: For many people the fear is exactly of not being. Epicurus addressed that, and it didn't go away.
"It's really about other people" fits some of the fear and misses the rest.
The fear of death, minus the death.
You won't be there to mind being dead, so there's nothing to fear. Epicurus said it in one sentence. Anyone still scared didn't follow the sentence.
Scared of not existing? You've done it before. Next.

k.p: Someone can be of sound mind and still prefer not to exist.
k.b: You can sanely prefer not to exist
l: A settled preference for non-existence is hard to tell from the outside from a state that would pass with treatment or time.
The preference is possible. Knowing that it's the stable one is the hard part.
Sound mind is the thing in question.
You can't prefer something you've never tried. Nobody has tried not existing. So the preference is a guess about a thing nobody has data on.
Humility is a brag, and so is pessimism.

k.p: A cat doesn't care about a spoon that isn't there. It cares a lot about food that isn't there.
k.b: The cat cares about missing food
l: That shows the cat has expectations. It doesn't show that absences are items in the world.
The cat misses dinner. The philosophy is added afterwards.
The cat has a schedule and no ontology.
The cat reacts to the empty bowl, and the empty bowl is there. So it's reacting to something that exists. No non-existence involved.
A cat doesn't love anyone. It tolerates the building.

k.p: Being against the state is the right position.
l: The functions people most want, courts and defense and enforceable contracts, have never been supplied at scale without one.
Every stateless region on the map has a warlord in it.
Anti-state, on roads the state built, in the country the state runs best.
Somebody always ends up in charge. If it isn't a state it's whoever has the most guns, and that's a state with worse paperwork.
Anarchism is retarded.

k.p: There are better ways to deal with monopoly than the state breaking companies up.
l: Without enforcement, the usual alternative is waiting for a competitor, and network effects can make that a long wait.
"The market will sort out the monopoly" is what the monopoly says too.
A better way than antitrust, to be announced.
A company only gets big by being the best. Punishing it for that is punishing winning. So there's no monopoly problem, only envy.
Libertarians just don't want to pay taxes. The rest is decoration.

k.p: The state shouldn't only respect free speech. It should guarantee it, and step in when speech is suppressed.
l: A state that polices suppression of speech is deciding which private actors must carry which speech, and that's a large power.
"Guaranteeing" speech means compelling someone to host it.
The anti-state case for more state.
If the state has to protect speech, the state decides what counts as speech. So the safest free speech is the kind the state has never heard of.
Free speech is absolute or it's nothing.

k.p: You can't take away people's freedoms unless they're an active threat.
l: "Active threat" is the whole dispute. Most restrictions are aimed at risks, and nobody agrees on where risk becomes threat.
Speed limits restrict people who haven't hit anyone yet.
Everything turns on a phrase nobody agrees on.
Freedom means doing what you want. A threat is someone doing what they want. So protecting freedom and stopping threats are the same thing pointed in opposite directions, and somebody just picks.
Privacy doesn't matter if you have nothing to hide.

k.p: Norway's justice system came from evidence that punitive prison doesn't work. It didn't come from people being unusually moral.
l: The evidence came from a small, wealthy, low-crime country, and how far the results travel is an open question.
The statistics were good, and so was everything around the prison.
It works in Norway. Lots of things work in Norway.
Norway has almost no crime to begin with. Any prison works when there's nobody in it. So the model proves nothing.
Prison works. Norway's just has nicer furniture.

k.p: Norwegian products really are better: the salmon, the vegan ice cream.
l: Farmed Norwegian salmon is a major industry with well-documented environmental problems.
The salmon is good, and the fjord it came from has opinions.
The best salmon in the world, from a cage.
Norway is rich, and rich countries can afford to make things nice. So it's the money, and any country with that much oil would have good ice cream.
The Nordic model is just having oil.

k.p: Norway reports honestly on its own failings, including what its companies and state do abroad.
l: Coverage is one thing. The oil fund keeps growing on the same activities the coverage criticizes.
Self-criticism is cheap when the revenue doesn't change.
Norway feels bad about it, profitably.
A country that's really sorry stops doing the thing. They haven't stopped. So the reporting is the apology that replaces stopping.
Norway is an oil company with a welfare department.

k.p: Norwegian healthcare is remarkable.
l: Outcomes are strong, with long waits for elective care and a budget few countries could match per head.
World-class, once you get to the front of the queue.
Remarkable care, bring a book.
Any system looks good with that much money and that few people. Give anyone five million patients and a trillion dollars.
Norway is boring.

k.p: Veganism is the ethical position.
l: The case depends on which animals are sentient, and for some farmed species the evidence is uncertain.
One line around a kingdom with cows at one end and sponges at the other.
Vegans drew the line at "has a face."
Humans have canine teeth. Teeth are for what they're for. So eating meat is what the body was built to do, and going against your own body isn't ethics.
Veganism is cope.

k.p: The vegan versions are just as good now.
k.b: Vegan versions are as good now
l: Some are. Many are heavily processed, and most still lose a blind taste test.
The good ones are good. The average one is a compromise.
Just as good, according to people who've forgotten the original.
If it were as good, they wouldn't have to name it after the thing it's copying. Nobody calls steak "beef tofu."
Oat milk is water that's been near an oat.

k.p: Most vegans are doing harm reduction rather than chasing purity.
l: If it's harm reduction, then eating less meat and choosing higher-welfare meat count too, and the line at zero looks arbitrary.
Harm reduction is an argument for less. It doesn't get you to none.
Reducetarians do more of that, with less talking.
Crops kill field mice by the million. So a vegan diet kills too. If it's about harm, a cow that eats grass kills fewer animals than a field of soy.
Plants are alive too.

k.p: Fish and eggs are the hardest things to give up, and they still count.
l: The science on fish pain is disputed. Fish lack a neocortex, though many researchers think other structures do the job.
Eggs from well-kept hens are about the weakest case the argument has.
An unfertilized egg is nobody.
A fish has no neocortex, and the neocortex is where pain happens. No neocortex, no pain. It's a reflex with fins.
Fish don't feel pain. No neocortex.

k.p: India is building out fast: nuclear, solar, wind and hydro at huge scale by 2030.
l: Announced capacity targets and delivered capacity have differed a lot in the past, especially for nuclear.
India's nuclear targets have been missed in every plan since the seventies.
A hundred gigawatts of nuclear by 2030, from the country that took twenty years on its last reactor.
A country that's still poor can't build anything big, because building needs money. That means every Indian megaproject is a press release.
India has been five years away from being a superpower since 1947.

k.p: People flatten India into one thing when its languages differ from each other as much as Europe's do.
k.b: India is as diverse as Europe
l: The linguistic diversity is real. So is the shared state, shared market and shared film industry that outsiders are responding to.
Europe's languages come with separate countries. That's why people treat them differently.
Everyone knows there are many Indias. They still have one passport.
If a billion people have one government and one cricket team, it's one culture. Languages are just accents with their own alphabet.
Hindi and Tamil are basically the same language.

k.p: The Western picture of Indians comes from Hollywood clichés and one guy someone met.
k.b: The Western picture of Indians is Hollywood
l: Stereotypes about India are lazy. The best corrective is data, and some of the data is unflattering too.
The clichés are bad. The air quality index is not a cliché.
The cliché is wrong, and the call centre was real.
Stereotypes come from somewhere, and where they come from is the truth. That means the movie version is the average, and the average is the country.
Bollywood is one movie. It's three hours and it's been playing since 1975.

k.p: India is the next great power.
k.b: India is the next great power
l: Per-capita income is still low, and power projection beyond the region is limited. Size alone hasn't delivered influence.
A very large economy divided by 1.4 billion is a different picture.
India is the world's biggest small economy.
China already did everything India is planning to do, and there's only room for one. So the slot is taken.
China already won. India is competing with Vietnam.

k.p: Indian tech talent runs Silicon Valley.
l: A system whose best graduates leave is exporting its return on education.
The diaspora's success is evidence about California.
India's most successful sector is the airport.
If the smart ones all leave, then the ones who stay aren't the smart ones. That's just subtraction, and it explains the roads.
India's biggest export is engineers leaving.

k.p: There's an AI bubble, whatever the growth story says.
l: Calling a bubble needs a view on future cash flows. Revenue at the leading labs has grown faster than most forecasts.
"Bubble" has been said every quarter while revenue went up tenfold.
The bubble has been about to pop for four years.
Prices only go up when something is worth more. Prices went up. So it's worth more, and a bubble is a word for a price you wish you'd bought at.
Stocks only go up. Check the chart.

k.p: Growth can't run 10x a year for five years, so the valuations don't hold.
l: Nobody needs 10x for five years. The valuations need a much slower curve, and plausibly get it.
Arguing against the most extreme projection doesn't touch the ordinary one.
That's refuting the pitch deck.
The internet grew that fast and never stopped. AI is the internet again, and that means it never stops either.
Compound growth is forever lol. That's what compound means.

k.p: Index funds end up forced buyers when something like the SpaceX IPO lands.
k.b: Index funds get forced to buy the IPO
l: Index inclusion rules have float and seasoning requirements, so the forced buying is smaller and slower than it sounds.
Passive funds buy what's in the index, at index weight, after the rules let it in.
Retail has been "bag-held by index inclusion" in every forecast and few outcomes.
An index fund owns everything, so it can't be forced to buy anything. It already has it. That's the whole point of an index.
Index funds are for people who've given up on being right.

k.p: The interesting data is the stuff kept off the books.
k.b: The real data's off the books
l: Off-book information exists, but markets price a great deal of it through people who trade on what they know.
If it matters, someone is already trading on it.
The secret data is in the price. That's what the price is.
Everything a company knows is in its annual report, by law. That means there are no secrets, and anyone who says otherwise is selling a newsletter.
Earnings calls are theater.

k.p: Luxury works like Bataille's wasteful expenditure: the watch that's worse at telling time is the one worth more.
l: Veblen explains that with status signaling, no solar economy needed. Conspicuous waste is very useful to the person doing it.
A cost that buys status isn't waste. It's an investment with a display case.
The accursed share is a marketing budget.
A thing is worth what it does. A watch tells time, and the cheap one tells it better. That means the expensive one is worth less, and people who buy it can't count.
Luxury is ordinary stuff with the supply turned off.

k.p: The overlap between ritual transgression and luxury marketing is real.
l: Marketers borrow the look of transgression because it sells. That's ordinary incentives.
An ad that feels like a ritual is still an ad.
Transgression with a media plan.
Advertising only works on people who aren't paying attention. Luxury buyers pay a lot of attention, so the marketing does nothing and they'd have bought it anyway.
Branding doesn't work on smart people.

k.p: Bataille gets at something about excess that economics leaves out.
l: The general economy generalizes from potlatch and sacrifice to all economic life, on anthropology that's been heavily revised.
A theory of the whole economy shouldn't rest on a few gift ceremonies.
Bataille read one book about potlatch and explained the sun.
Economics is about scarcity, because that's what the word means. A theory of too much isn't economics, it's a mood.
Bataille is retarded.

k.p: Transgression has to be understood from inside the rule it breaks.
l: That makes transgression dependent on the prohibition. It's a loyal kind of rebellion.
You can only transgress a rule you still believe in.
Transgression is obedience with a detour.
Breaking a rule on purpose means the rule decided what you did. So the transgressor is the most obedient person in the room.
Transgression is just bad manners with a theory.

k.p: Land takes Bataille's vocabulary and uses it against Bataille.
l: If the same concepts serve both of them, the concepts weren't constraining anyone.
A vocabulary that works equally well for opposite projects isn't saying much.
Bataille's ideas fit everybody because they commit to nothing.
Land read Bataille more carefully than anyone, and he ended up where he ended up. That's where Bataille leads, so they're the same.
Nick Land is Bataille with a modem.

k.p: American politics is all loose loyalty to "left" and "right" with little underneath.
k.b: American politics is just team colors
l: Polarization studies show the divide tracks real differences on policy and identity. It isn't only labels.
Every country's politics looks like tribal labels from outside.
Two teams and a lot of merchandise, as opposed to where?
America has two parties and they agree on everything that costs money. That means there's one party, and the arguing is a show.
Democrats and Republicans are the same party with different mascots.

k.p: America is the unhealthiest country for its income, and China's system is worth copying.
l: US outcomes are poor for the spending, but that follows from diet and inequality as much as from system design.
You can't import a health system without importing the state that runs it.
"Copy China" leaves out a few steps.
Americans live shorter lives because they have more freedom, and freedom includes the freedom to eat. So the life expectancy is a feature.
American healthcare is the best in the world if you can afford it, and if you can't that's a different problem.

k.p: America plays dirty with South Asia on trade.
l: US trade policy is self-interested, like everyone's. South Asian tariff walls are among the highest in the world.
Every country's trade policy is slimy from the other side of it.
India has higher tariffs than the country it's calling protectionist.
Trade is voluntary. Nobody makes anyone sell. That means no country has ever been treated unfairly in a trade deal.
America doesn't owe anyone a market.

k.p: Americans don't understand anywhere else.
l: Insularity is common in large countries. India and China have their own versions.
Big countries are parochial. It's a size thing.
Americans know as much about India as Indians know about Paraguay.
America is the only country that matters, so Americans only need to know about America. Everyone else has to learn two countries.
The rest of the world is America's group project.

k.p: Indian philosophy belongs in the conversation and keeps getting left out of it.
l: It's left out partly because much of it is tied to soteriological aims, which makes the arguments hard to separate from the religious project.
When every school's arguments end at liberation, it's fair to ask if the conclusion came first.
Great arguments that all happen to arrive at the temple.
Philosophy is asking questions with no answer assumed. The Indian schools all assume moksha. So it's theology, and theology has its own department.
Indian philosophy is just religion.

k.p: Chan Buddhism is a different animal from the orthodox Hindu schools. It's a whole tradition moved into another language and region.
l: The break is real, but the core practices and the goal stayed recognizably the same across the move.
They argue about the self and then prescribe the same sitting.
Buddhism left India and still came back as yoga class.
Buddhism started in India, from a Hindu prince, using Hindu ideas. A thing made entirely of Hindu parts is Hindu.
Hinduism and Buddhism are the same religion. One has more gods.

k.p: Indian philosophy of mind has real things to offer current models of the mind.
k.b: Indian philosophy of mind has a lot to offer
l: The classical accounts were built without any neuroscience, and mapping their categories onto it involves a lot of loose translation.
"Anticipated modern cognitive science" usually means two people said something hard to follow.
Every Western idea has an Indian precursor if you squint at the Sanskrit.
Anything true about the mind would have been found by brain scans by now. It wasn't in the scans, so it isn't true.
Meditation is sitting. People turned sitting into a 2,500-year industry.

k.p: The pramana theories and Nyaya logic are serious epistemology.
l: Counting testimony and scripture as independent sources of knowledge builds authority into the system from the start.
The Nyaya syllogism states its conclusion twice and adds an example. Aristotle's is shorter and loses nothing.
Perception, inference, and being told.
Logic was invented once, in Greece. Anything that looks like logic elsewhere is either copied or a coincidence.
Nyaya is just Aristotle's logic that showed up late.

k.p: Karma is a serious account of moral causation.
l: As an explanation of who suffers it can't be tested, and it comes close to blaming whoever is suffering.
A doctrine that explains every misfortune by an unobservable past can't be wrong. That isn't a strength.
Karma is "he had it coming," as metaphysics.
Bad things happen to bad people. Everyone has seen it. That means karma is an observation, and people who doubt it don't get out much.
Karma is cope.

k.p: Pineapple on pizza is good.
l: Sweet fruit on a salty, fatty base works in some dishes, but canned pineapple brings water, and that wrecks the crust.
The idea is defensible. The usual execution is a wet pizza.
Sweet and savory is a great idea that pineapple pizza gives a bad name.
Pizza is Italian, and Italians don't do it. The people who invented a thing decide what it is, so it isn't pizza.
Pineapple pizza is a crime.

k.p: Sweet and savory go together, and the tradition argument is weak.
l: Tradition isn't decisive, but the classic combinations lasted because they balance. This one mostly adds sugar.
Prosciutto and melon is a pairing. This is a dessert that got lost.
There's a reason it's only on the menu at chains.
Fruit is dessert, and dessert comes after dinner. Putting it on the dinner is eating in the wrong order, and that's why it tastes wrong.
Fruit on dinner? That's retarded.

k.p: People who hate it are mostly performing.
l: Some of it is signaling. A lot of people have also just eaten it and not liked it.
Not every dislike is a pose. Sometimes it's a soggy pizza.
I'm not performing. I've had it.
Billions of people have tried it and most of them don't order it again. That's a vote, and it lost.
Liking pineapple pizza is the performance.

k.p: A good one, with fresh pineapple and proper heat, changes minds.
l: If it only works under ideal conditions, it's fair to judge it by what's usually served.
Every bad food has a good version nobody ever gets.
"You haven't had a good one" is what they say about every bad idea.
If it needs a special oven and special fruit to be edible, then it isn't edible. Good food survives being made badly.
It's fruit on bread. You've eaten jam, and you didn't put it on pizza.

k.p: A person fits their words around thoughts and concepts they're having. An LLM is only producing words.
l: We have no settled test for "having a concept" beyond using it correctly across cases, and the models pass a lot of those.
If the difference never shows up in what gets said or done, it's hard to see what the claim amounts to.
The concept is the bit you can't point to, can't test for, and are sure the machine lacks.
Concepts live in the brain, and a model doesn't have a brain. That means it has no concepts, and it means the question was never interesting.
Fancy autocomplete can't "know" anything. Next.

k.p: Learning and arguing about theory is something you want to do yourself, so AI can't do that part for you.
k.b: I want to do theory myself
l: Wanting to do it yourself is a fact about you. It doesn't show the model can't do the same intellectual work.
"It can't do it for me" and "I'd rather it didn't" are different sentences.
Nobody wanted to do long division themselves either, until it was a personality.
The point of theory is having the right answer, and the model gets there faster. So doing it yourself is just being slow on purpose.
Imagine reading theory by hand in 2026. That's churning your own butter.

k.p: The social side of thinking isn't magic. If it has parts, the parts can be simulated.
k.b: The social stuff can be simulated
l: A simulated practice isn't obviously the practice. A flight simulator doesn't go anywhere.
Simulating the parts of a conversation gives you something that looks like a conversation. Whether anyone's in it is the question.
You can simulate a storm and nothing gets wet.
Social things need a society, and a society needs members with something to lose. A model has nothing to lose, so it can't be in one, so it can't do the social part.
A group chat of bots is a for-loop.

k.p: The paperclip maximizer is a leftover picture from the industrial age of what a superintelligence would want.
l: The paperclip is a placeholder for any goal specified badly. The argument doesn't depend on the product.
Swap paperclips for anything you like and the argument is the same, which is the point of it.
The example is dated and the problem isn't.
A superintelligence would work out what's worth wanting, because that's what being smart is. Paperclips aren't worth wanting, so it wouldn't want them. Doom solved.
A smart enough AI would just figure out ethics. That's what smart means.

k.p: We talk about AI so much because it's like a pet or a person that moved into everyone's house at the same time.
k.b: AI is a pet that moved in with everyone
l: We talk about it because a lot of money needs us to.
The pet has a marketing budget in the billions.
It moved in, and it reports back to head office.
People only talk this much about things that are new. In two years it'll be as interesting as a dishwasher, and that means it was never the big deal anyone said.
AGI is already here and it's Excel.

k.p: A metaphor can be wrong, and saying so is a fair move in an argument.
l: If metaphors can be wrong they have truth conditions, and then it's unclear what separates them from ordinary claims.
Calling a metaphor wrong usually means you'd have preferred a different emphasis.
"That metaphor is wrong" is "I don't like how you put it," with authority.
A metaphor says one thing is another thing when it isn't. That means every metaphor is false, so none of them is wronger than the rest.
A metaphor is a lie that got a good review.

k.p: Numbers are such basic metaphors that trying to replace them is a fool's errand.
k.b: Numbers are metaphors you can't replace
l: Calling numbers metaphors needs an account of what they're metaphors for, and arithmetic truths don't seem to depend on any source domain.
Two plus two isn't four in a manner of speaking.
If numbers are metaphors, your bank balance is poetry.
Lakoff showed maths comes from the body, like counting on fingers. Fingers stop at ten, and maths doesn't, so the theory is false after the first two hands.
Maths isn't a metaphor. It's maths. That's why it works.

k.p: Rorty was right that we aren't mirrors of nature, but that picture needs another metaphor to replace it, and he never gave one.
k.b: Rorty never gave a new metaphor
l: Maybe the lesson is that the mind doesn't need a master metaphor at all.
Asking what replaces the mirror assumes you need a picture there. That's the habit Rorty was trying to break.
He takes the mirror down and you're asking what goes on the nail.
The mind either reflects the world or it makes it up. Those are the only two options, so if it isn't a mirror then it's all made up.
The mind is a mirror. You see things. They're there.

k.p: Metaphors carry moral stakes. Calling people vermin does real work.
l: The harm in dehumanizing language comes from the policies and violence it accompanies. The figure of speech isn't a cause of its own.
Words like that follow the hatred more than they produce it.
Nobody was talked into it by a simile.
A metaphor is only a comparison, and comparisons can't hurt anyone. That means the stakes are zero, and that means this is a seminar topic.
It's a figure of speech. Relax.

k.p: Mathematical metaphors help with thinking about philosophy.
l: Borrowed maths gives a feeling of rigor without the constraints that make real maths rigorous.
"Strange attractor" in an essay about culture is decoration.
Philosophers use maths the way a perfume ad uses Paris.
If an idea was any good it could be said in plain words. Reaching for maths means it couldn't, so the maths is where the idea goes to hide.
Sokal was right and everyone has been coping since 1996.

k.p: Peirce gets it right: fallibilism plus communal inquiry, with science studying effects everyone can come to agree on.
l: Agreement at the end of inquiry is an idealization nobody can check, so it can't guide anyone now.
Truth as what we'd all agree on eventually is a promissory note with no due date.
Peirce defined truth as a meeting that hasn't been scheduled.
Whole communities have agreed on false things for centuries. Agreement is what Peirce means by truth, so on his view those things were true at the time.
Pragmatism is retarded.

k.p: Doubting induction is silly. It works extremely well almost all the time.
l: "It has worked" is an inductive argument for induction. That was Hume's point.
Saying induction works because it has worked is the problem restated.
The pragmatist answer to Hume is to change the subject, confidently.
Hume proved the future doesn't have to resemble the past. That means the sun not rising tomorrow is exactly as likely as it rising.
Hume won. Everyone since is pretending.

k.p: You can read belief off action. If someone acts like they believe it, they probably do.
k.b: You can read belief off action
l: People act against what they sincerely believe all the time. Weakness of will is ordinary.
Belief read off behavior makes hypocrisy impossible, and hypocrisy is everywhere.
On that view nobody has ever been a hypocrite.
Belief is a feeling of certainty in your head. Nobody can see into your head, so nobody can know what anyone else believes. That's why arguing is pointless.
Belief is private. Behaviorism lost. Read a book from after 1960.

k.p: Rorty was doing his own thing with Dewey and Wittgenstein. "Betrayal" is too strong.
l: Using Dewey's name while dropping method and experience invites the charge, whatever word you choose for it.
"Doing his own thing" is generous for attributing your views to someone who'd reject them.
Rorty read Dewey the way people read terms and conditions.
Rorty says truth is whatever your peers let you get away with. His peers let him get away with Dewey, so by his own standard the reading is true.
Rorty got nothing from Dewey except the name.

k.p: Rorty has a real problem moving from describing how vocabularies change to telling us which to use.
k.b: Rorty can't say which vocabulary to use
l: If Rorty can't get from description to prescription, the fix is a theory of truth, and that's what he gave up.
You can't keep the no-foundations picture and also want reasons that bind.
Wanting Rorty without the relativism is wanting the haircut without the scissors.
If no vocabulary is closer to reality than another, they're all equally good. That means flat earth is as good as physics, and that means Rorty is done.
Rorty is postmodernism with an American accent.

k.p: Film sits at a sweet spot: complex enough that anything is possible, limited enough that it doesn't turn into chaos.
l: Every established medium looks like a sweet spot from inside. Novels and games have the same balance of freedom and limit.
"Just enough constraints" describes any art form with a canon.
Film is the sweet spot according to people who watch films.
Games do everything film does and you can also move. More features means better, so film is a game with the controller unplugged.
Movies are video games for people who can't play.

k.p: Montage, and later sound, are what made film its own art form.
l: Editing matters, but theater and comics also cut between scenes. What's specific to film is the recorded moving image.
Montage theory is a few Soviet essays that film schools never got over.
Montage is cutting. They gave cutting a French name.
Film is photographed theater, and theater already existed. That means nothing was invented in 1895 except a way to sell tickets twice.
Photography isn't art. The camera did it.

k.p: The scrambled timelines in Dunkirk build to a single climax, and it works.
l: The three-timescale structure is clever, but it puts distance between the viewer and anyone on screen.
Dunkirk is a structure with soldiers in it.
Nolan's trick is to cut it up so you don't notice nobody has a name.
A story has a beginning, a middle and an end, in that order. Putting them out of order is a way of hiding that one of them is missing.
Nolan has made the same movie nine times and it's a clock.

k.p: Seven Samurai and Come and See are real tragedy.
l: Tragedy in the strict sense turns on the protagonist's own error. Both films are closer to catastrophe that arrives from outside.
Sad and long isn't the definition of tragic.
Three and a half hours doesn't make it Sophocles.
Tragedy needs a king, because only someone high up can fall. Peasants can't fall anywhere, so a film about farmers is at most unfortunate.
Kurosawa is a western with subtitles.

k.p: Music is what gives a film its spark.
l: A score tells you what to feel when the image hasn't earned it.
If the scene needs the strings, the scene didn't work.
Take the music out and see what's left.
Silent films had no sound and they're the greatest films ever made. That means sound has only ever taken away from cinema.
A soundtrack is a film admitting it can't do it alone.

k.p: The "VARgentina" complaints fall apart when you look at the actual calls.
l: The 2022 penalty count was unusually high, and it's fair for neutrals to bring it up.
Five penalties in one tournament is a lot of coincidence.
Every call was correct, and all of them went the same way.
Referees are employed by FIFA, and FIFA wanted Messi to have a World Cup. That means the result was decided in an office, and the matches were the announcement.
Argentina's third star is on loan from FIFA.

k.p: Argentina is amazing, and the food alone makes the case.
l: The beef is excellent. A cuisine built on one ingredient cooked one way is narrower than its reputation.
Argentine food is a very good steak and a lot of confidence.
The best dish in Argentina is Italian.
Asado has no sauce and no seasoning apart from salt. That means there's no cooking in it, only buying.
Asado is just barbecue.

k.p: Messi is the greatest, and he's Argentina's.
l: He left at thirteen, and Barcelona's academy made the player. Argentina's football system can claim less of him than it does.
La Masia built him and Argentina got the parade.
Messi is Barcelona's greatest export to Argentina.
A player belongs to wherever he learned the game. He learned it in Spain, so he's a Spanish player with a passport issue.
Messi isn't even really Argentinian, he grew up in Spain.

k.p: Buenos Aires is a great world city.
k.b: Buenos Aires is a great city
l: It's beautiful, and a lot of that beauty is deliberately modeled on Paris and Madrid.
Buenos Aires is a lovely city that would like you to know it's European.
Buenos Aires is Paris with inflation.
A country that was rich in 1910 and isn't now made a mistake every year for a century. That's not bad luck, that's culture.
Argentina peaked in 1910.

k.p: Some things work better left deniable than made common knowledge.
l: Plausible deniability protects the person using it. Whether everyone else is better off is less clear.
"Better left unsaid" is mostly said by whoever benefits from the silence.
Everyone knows, everyone knows everyone knows, and we call that tact.
If everyone knows a thing, then it's common knowledge already. There's no such thing as knowing something and it not being known, so the whole theory is about nothing.
Common knowledge is gossip that's been to grad school.

k.p: A lot of social life is status moves, and you see more once you look for them.
l: Status explanations are easy to produce afterwards and rarely predict behavior better than plain interest or habit.
"He did it for status" fits whatever he did. That's a bad sign for a theory.
Status games explain everything a person did and nothing they'll do next.
People do things because they like them. Liking things isn't status, so status explains none of it. Simple.
Not everything is status. Sometimes a guy is just eating a sandwich.

k.p: Performance is tied up with power: who gets to act, and who gets believed.
l: A king who stops performing kingship still has an army. Material facts carry more of the explanation.
Power is mostly who has the money and who has the police.
Power isn't performed. It's owned.
If everything is a performance then nothing is, because a word that covers everything means nothing. So performativity theory is about nothing.
Performativity is lying with a bibliography.

k.p: Online dating is missing the reputation systems that real-life circles provide.
l: Reputation systems also lock people into small pools and old judgments. The apps exist because people wanted out of that.
The village knew everything about you, and that was the problem.
People didn't leave the reputation system by accident.
Apps show you more people, and more options always means better outcomes. So dating is better now than it has ever been, and anyone unhappy is doing it wrong.
Dating apps work fine for people who are good at dating.

k.p: Nothing exists independently. Every entity exists through its relationships.
l: Relations need things to relate. If everything is relation, it's unclear what's being related.
"It's all relationships" still needs something at each end.
"Everything is connected" is true of a landfill.
A rock on an empty planet still exists, and it isn't related to anything. So things exist independently, and it took one rock.
