Metaphysics is just semantics.

k.p: Separation isn't an illusion. It's an adaptive abstraction over a relational reality.
l: If separateness is adaptive, it's tracking something real about where one thing ends and another begins.
An abstraction that works every single time is usually called a fact.
The abstraction has been right about where my hand ends for my whole life.
If it helps you survive, it's true. That's what evolution selects for. So separation is true and the relational part is the abstraction.
Everything is separate lol. That's why there's more than one thing.

k.p: We should preserve relationships because we want things to flourish, with resilience first.
l: "Flourishing" needs a standard. What keeps a system going and what's good are different claims.
Resilience is a property parasites have too.
Flourishing is a nice word for "still here."
Whatever survives is what flourished. So the ethics says: be whatever's left. That's a description of the winners.
Humanity doesn't have a telos. Neither does yeast.

k.p: The grounding is the long-term flourishing of the system that lets us be conscious at all.
k.b: Flourishing of the system grounds it
l: That's a commitment a person can hold. It doesn't follow from any description of the system.
Ecology tells you how systems behave. It doesn't say which ones to want.
The is-ought gap doesn't close because something was planted in it.
The system doesn't care whether we're in it. It ran for three billion years with nobody reflecting on it. So it can't be the ground of anything we owe.
Ecology is just "everything affects everything," which is true and useless.

k.p: Physics points the same way: entanglement and the rest suggest a relational reality.
l: Entanglement is a specific, well-understood correlation. It doesn't support claims about meaning or connection between people.
Quantum mechanics gets borrowed for a lot of things it doesn't say.
Entanglement is two particles, in a lab, at near absolute zero.
Quantum effects only happen at tiny scales. People are big. So nothing quantum has anything to do with people, ever.
Entanglement is two gloves in two boxes.

k.p: Evil is a human construct, one pole of a dualism.
l: If evil is only a construct, there's nothing for a framework of flourishing to be against.
A relational ethics needs some things to be really bad for the system.
Evil is a construct, and here are the things we must correct.
If evil is made up then so is good, since they come as a pair. Then nothing is better than anything, and no manifesto is needed.
Morality is subjective.

k.p: Those who degrade the system should face real corrective action. Fines aren't enough.
l: "Corrective action" beyond fines needs someone with the authority to decide what counts as degradation, and that's a lot of power.
Someone has to hold the list of who's degrading the system.
Reducing people's power for the good of the whole has a history.
Everybody degrades the system a little just by being alive. So everyone qualifies for correction, and it comes down to who's holding the clipboard.
Every utopia has a department of corrective action.

k.p: People who disagree about abortion or even murder aren't like flat-earthers. Moral disagreement is a different thing.
l: If moral disagreement isn't like factual error, it's unclear what makes the flourishing framework more than one preference among others.
Either there's something to be right about, or the framework is a taste.
You can't have "not like facts" and "you should adopt my framework" together.
Flat-earthers are wrong because we can check. You can't check a moral. So morals are opinions, and opinions can't be wrong.
Ethics is cheering.

k.p: Consciousness is a gift and should be treated like one.
l: A gift has a giver. Without one, "gift" is a way of saying you're glad of it, and that's fine but it isn't an argument.
Gratitude is a good attitude and a weak premise.
A gift from whom?
Nobody gave it to us. It evolved because it helped apes not get eaten. You don't owe anyone for a thing that happened by accident.
Consciousness is just the brain.

k.p: We're conscious through evolution. AI is simulated consciousness, and the difference matters.
l: If what matters is the process that produced it, the claim needs an account of why origin, and not organization, makes experience.
"Evolved" tells you how it got here. It doesn't tell you what it is.
Being born the old-fashioned way is doing a lot of work.
A simulation of a thing isn't the thing. A simulated fire doesn't burn. So simulated consciousness is no consciousness, and that's the end of it.
AI is a tool. Tools don't deserve respect. Nobody thanks a hammer.

k.p: AI only goes as far as its user. What it makes is a synthesis of existing ideas.
k.b: AI only goes as far as its user
l: The same is true of people, as the claim itself usually admits. Then it isn't a limit specific to AI.
"Only recombines what exists" describes every human who ever wrote anything.
It only remixes, like every artist's influences section.
A machine can only give back what was put in. Nobody put in anything new, because new things don't exist yet. So it can't produce anything new, by definition.
It read the whole internet and still has nothing to say.

k.p: Handing your relationships over to AI is corrosive for society.
k.b: Outsourcing relationships to AI is bad
l: People said the same of novels, telephones and television. The evidence so far is mixed.
Every new medium has been the end of human connection.
The telephone was going to do this too.
People are free to talk to whoever they like. If they like the machine better, that's a review of the people.
Online friends aren't real friends, and neither is this.

k.p: Generating art from artists' scraped work is wrong.
l: Human artists learn from others' work without permission too. The harm case rests on scale and the market, and learning as such isn't the problem.
Every art student has trained on unlicensed data.
Influence was fine until it got fast.
Looking at a picture isn't stealing it. The model looked at pictures. So nothing was stolen, and artists are upset about being looked at.
Art is whatever sells.

k.p: Ecological collapse is the central problem of this century.
k.b: Ecological collapse is the big one
l: It's among the most serious, and treating it as the one master problem can crowd out others with firmer evidence on timing.
Central is a ranking, and rankings need the comparison shown.
Every generation has had a central problem.
People have predicted collapse every decade since the seventies, and here we are. After fifty years of being wrong, you stop being a forecast.
Doom is a genre.

k.p: Nature's cycles are something we should fit ourselves into.
l: Much of natural history is directional: extinction, irreversible change. The cycles are a selective reading.
Nature has seasons, and it also has mass extinctions that didn't come back round.
The dinosaurs are still waiting for their turn in the cycle.
Fitting into nature is how people used to live, and they died at thirty. Everything good since came from not fitting in.
Nature isn't cyclical. It's a line, and it goes down.

k.p: Societies that never reach an ethic of flourishing may be the ones that go extinct.
l: That's a hypothesis about selection with no cases to check it against.
A sample of zero civilizations supports any theory.
The Fermi paradox, solved by the view I already hold.
If good ethics made civilizations survive, the nicest ones in history would still be here. The ones still here are the ones with the biggest armies.
Resilience is just not dying yet.

k.p: The earth can be harmed, and we're harming it.
l: Organisms and ecosystems are harmed. The planet's processes carry on, so "harming the earth" is a metaphor for harm to living things.
Saving the planet means saving conditions good for us.
The earth has had worse than us and didn't keep a diary.
A rock can't be hurt. The earth is a big rock. So it can't be hurt, and the only thing in danger is our own comfort.
The earth isn't a person. It doesn't get hurt. It's a rock with weather.

k.p: A law could have a rare alternative outcome that simply never happened, and we'd never know.
k.b: A law could have a hidden exception
l: A chance that never shows up in trillions of trials is indistinguishable from no chance. The simpler law wins.
A one percent chance that never happens isn't one percent.
A hidden branch that never fires is a zero with a story.
If it never happens, it can't happen. That's what never means. So the law doesn't have the exception, and the universe isn't hiding one.
Laws of nature are just habits the universe hasn't broken yet.

k.p: Water boiling and a die landing are alike. Each is just a result that happens in the world.
k.b: Boiling water and dice are alike
l: One follows from conditions we can state and control. The other is sensitive to conditions we can't measure. That difference matters.
You can boil water on purpose.
Nobody has ever rolled a six by turning up the heat.
A die roll is physics too. Throw it exactly the same way and you get the same number. So nothing is random, including the die.
A dice roll isn't random, it's lazy physics.

k.p: Things look uniform to us because we only see the macro result. The micro level could be doing something else.
k.b: We only see the macro level
l: Macro regularity is what laws describe. Unobservable micro variation that averages out makes no difference to them.
If it averages out perfectly, it's not doing anything.
Could be anything down there, as long as it sums to the same thing.
If we can only see the macro level, then the macro level is all there is evidence for. The rest is imagination.
Infinity isn't a number, so nothing is infinite.

k.p: An exact atomic copy, with different atoms in the same arrangement, raises the real question about who that is.
k.b: An exact copy raises the real question
l: If pattern is what matters, the copy is as good as the original. If it isn't, something beyond pattern needs naming.
Either the pattern is you or you owe us a soul.
Same arrangement, different atoms. That's also you compared with last year.
You don't have the atoms you were born with. Nobody held a funeral. So the atoms never mattered and the copy is you.
The teleporter is fine. Atoms get replaced every seven years anyway.

k.p: Resurrection doesn't have to mean coming back at the instant after death. Any point would count.
k.b: Resurrection can be at any point
l: If any stage counts, it's unclear which one is "the person." A four-year-old Einstein isn't the man who wrote the papers.
Pick an age and you've picked a different guy.
Resurrect him at four and you've got a kid who likes trains.
If you can bring him back at any age, you can bring him back at two ages at once. Then there's two. Two can't be one person.
Resurrection is just a copy with good timing.

k.p: With enough mastery of biology we could read off a brain's structure and rebuild it.
l: The information needed disperses at death, and entropy makes exact recovery a practical impossibility.
You can't unscramble the egg.
Thermodynamics has a view, and it's no.
The brain is a computer. Copy the file and that's the person. The only hard part is the cable.
The brain is a computer. Upload it and that's the person. Easy.

k.p: Reds only press red because they don't know the outcome. It isn't principle.
k.b: Reds only press red out of uncertainty
l: Acting on uncertainty about the outcome is a principle. It's prudence under risk, and decision theory is built on it.
Not knowing how it'll go is the situation, so it's a reasonable input.
"They only did it because of the stakes" describes most sensible decisions.
If you knew blue would win, you'd press blue. If you knew it would lose, you'd press red. So nobody votes on principle, and the blues are guessing with nicer language.
Red is retarded.

k.p: People should vote on principle, whatever the likely result.
l: A principle that ignores the likely result can cost lives for the sake of a gesture.
Principle without odds is how you get noble disasters.
"Regardless of outcome" is easy to say about other people's outcomes.
A vote that ignores what will happen is a vote for nothing happening the way you wanted. That's a diary entry.
Blue pressers are gambling with their life to feel like good people.

k.p: "I'll press red and use my life to do good" is a lie people tell themselves.
k.b: 'I'll do good with my life' is a lie
l: Some people would follow through. Predicting that none of them will is a guess about strangers.
Maybe. It's also unfalsifiable from here.
Everyone on the other side is lying to themselves, conveniently.
A living person can do good and a dead one can't. That's just true. So red does more good, and the tears are optional.
You can press red with tears in your eyes and still be right.

k.p: The subscription plans beat API pricing for nearly everyone.
k.b: Get the plan, not the API
l: The plans win until you reach the caps, and heavy users reach them mid-task.
Unlimited until Tuesday afternoon.
The plan is a great deal as long as you don't use it much.
Paying per token means paying for what you use, and that's always the fairest price. A flat plan means somebody is overpaying, and the house decides who.
API pricing is a scam and so is the plan.

k.p: The labs hook you on cheap access and raise the price once you depend on it.
k.b: They hook you then raise prices
l: Prices per token have dropped steeply over time. The dependence is real and the price trend is the opposite.
It's a strange dealer who keeps cutting the price.
First one's free, second one's also cheaper.
Companies can charge whatever they like, and they like more. So the price only ever goes up, and anyone who says it went down is looking at the wrong tab.
Claude won't help with anything fun, so it's a worse Google with opinions.

k.p: Somebody clever with a weak GPU in the middle of nowhere will unlock something big.
k.b: Some genius with a laptop GPU will crack it
l: Frontier results have tracked compute closely. Efficiency tricks tend to get absorbed by whoever has the most hardware.
The clever trick works, and then the big lab runs it at a thousand times the scale.
The lone genius with a laptop is a film.
Ideas are free and anyone can have one. Computers only run the idea. So the labs with the most computers have no advantage at all.
The next Steve Jobs is going to be an AI.

k.p: The hardware squeeze is real: GPUs are getting priced out of reach.
l: High-end prices rose, and capable used and mid-range cards are still widely available. The squeeze is at the top.
You can't afford the best card. You never could.
The squeeze is on people who wanted a datacenter at home.
Everything in computing gets cheaper every year. That's Moore's law, and it's a law. So GPUs are cheaper now and people complaining can't read a receipt.
Local models are for people who want to say they run local models.

k.p: Investing is important, and people should learn to do it.
l: Most active investors underperform a cheap index fund after fees. For most people, learning to invest means learning to stop picking.
The lesson of investing research is that the skill is mostly not doing it.
The average stock picker would do better by losing his password.
Nobody knows what a stock will do tomorrow. If nobody knows, it's chance, and a game of chance with money on it has a name.
Investing is gambling.

k.p: With a DCF you trust, you buy where the price sits well under the value.
l: A DCF is only as good as its growth and discount assumptions, and small changes swing the answer wildly.
A DCF tells you what you assumed, to two decimal places.
You can make a DCF say anything, and analysts do.
The price is what the whole market thinks it's worth. One guy with a spreadsheet can't know more than the whole market, so the DCF is always the one that's wrong.
DCF is fan fiction about a company's future.

k.p: A company trading below the cash and assets on its books is a bargain.
k.b: Below book value is a bargain
l: Assets on a balance sheet can be worth much less in practice, especially loans to borrowers who are already behind.
Cheap against book often means the market doesn't believe the book.
A bargain where the assets are other people's late car payments.
If it were really worth more than its price, someone richer would have bought it already. Nobody did. So it's worth less, and the balance sheet is fiction.
Imagine thinking you found a bargain the entire market missed lol.

k.p: Debt against an unstable cash flow is a trap.
k.b: Don't borrow on unstable cash flow
l: Debt is fine when the return on what it funds beats the interest. Stability matters less than the spread.
Never borrowing against uncertainty would rule out most businesses ever started.
No debt against unstable income: there goes every startup and half the farms.
Borrowed money is free until you pay it back, and you can always borrow more to do that. That means debt never has to cost anything.
Debt is a tool and poor people use it wrong.

k.p: If you invest well enough, you can buy out the bad ideas and kill them.
k.b: Invest well enough to kill bad ideas
l: Capital markets don't pick ideas by merit. Bad ideas with good margins get funded for decades.
The market kills unprofitable ideas, which isn't the same list as bad ones.
Investing your way to a better world, one ticker at a time.
Money goes to whatever makes money, and whatever makes money is what people want. So nothing that gets funded is a bad idea.
The stock market is a casino. Same thing. One has a dress code.

k.p: Technology is deflationary. It collapses costs.
l: Costs fall in the sectors technology touches, and the savings get spent elsewhere. The overall price level is set by money and demand.
TVs got cheap and rent didn't.
Technology is deflationary for things you can download.
Prices have gone up every year since computers were invented. So technology causes inflation. The chart is the chart.
Inflation is the government printing money. That's it. That's the whole field.

k.p: Debt is a way of building the economy out now, not just a burden to be inflated away later.
l: That holds when the borrowing funds productive assets. Much of it funds consumption and asset prices.
Debt builds the economy when it builds something.
Productive debt is lovely. Now look at what the debt bought.
A country that owes money is poorer than one that doesn't. The countries with the most debt are the richest ones. So debt makes you rich, and everyone should have as much as possible.
Loans are free money if you never plan to stop.

k.p: The way to beat inflation is to own productive assets.
l: That swaps inflation risk for market risk. In the short run, asset prices can fall while prices rise.
Stocks beat inflation over decades and can lose to it for one.
You beat inflation by owning stocks, the way you beat rain by owning a boat.
Inflation only hurts people who hold cash. Holding cash is a choice. So inflation is a tax on people who chose it.
Inflation only hurts people who hold cash, and that's their fault.

k.p: A lender that takes the property if you can't pay is on solid ground.
l: Collateral protects the lender when the asset holds its value. Property values fall in the same downturn that causes the defaults.
Secured lending is safe until the security is what went wrong.
The property is worth least exactly when you get it.
Houses never go down, because they aren't making more land. So a loan against a house can't lose, and that has been true every year except the ones people remember.
Yield is free. That's what makes it yield.

k.p: The dollar's position is shakier than people assume.
k.b: The dollar's shakier than you think
l: Its end has been announced regularly since 1971, and its share of reserves and trade is still dominant.
De-dollarization is always five years away.
The petrodollar is over and nobody told the price of oil.
Money is only worth what's behind it, and nothing is behind the dollar since 1971. So it has been worth nothing for fifty years and people haven't noticed.
Gold is the only real money and the rest is paper with a president on it.

k.p: "Lines of flight" is a useful idea: the ways out of a fixed arrangement.
l: The concept gives no way to tell a liberating exit from a destructive one. Deleuze admits lines of flight can go bad.
A line of flight is leaving, with no forwarding address.
Running away, with a bibliography.
A line goes from one place to another place. So a line of flight just ends up somewhere else that's also a place. Nothing has been escaped.
Deleuze is a fraud. A line of flight is a guy quitting his job.

k.p: You can treat it as an ethic: act so as to maximize lines of flight.
l: Maximizing exits says nothing about where to go, so it can't guide a choice between two exits.
"Keep your options open" isn't an ethics.
It's commitment issues with a universal law attached.
Kant's rule tells you what to do. This one tells you to keep being able to do other things. A rule that never picks anything isn't a rule.
"Deterritorialization" means moving.

k.p: You can be "schizo" about forces and capital, not just about people. That's the point of the books.
l: Using a clinical term as a model of liberation was careless then, and it has aged badly.
The metaphor needed a diagnosis to sound radical.
Anti-Oedipus is two men who liked a word.
A book that costs thirty dollars and is sold in shops is part of capitalism. So it can't be against capitalism. It's a product.
Capitalism and Schizophrenia has a price on the back.

k.p: After Deleuze died, everyone else was left holding the ball.
k.b: Deleuze died and left us the ball
l: The followers produced commentary more than new work. That says something about how usable the system was.
A philosophy that can only be glossed wasn't built to be used.
Sixty years of people explaining what he meant.
If the ideas were clear, nobody would need followers to interpret them. There are thousands of interpreters. That's the review.
Every Deleuzian is three books away from making a point.

k.p: Cities treat homeless people as an eyesore and then remove every place they could go.
k.b: Cities push the homeless out of everywhere
l: Cities face real conflicts over shared space. Tolerating camps hasn't improved outcomes for the people living in them.
Clearing a park and housing a person are separate jobs, and cities are bad at both.
The city is cruel, and the camp also isn't a solution.
Nobody is homeless in a town with cheap houses. So it's the price of houses, so it's building, so anyone talking about anything else is wasting time.
Homelessness is a housing problem. Build houses. It's in the name.

k.p: The homeless are people with skills and decency. Give them credit.
l: Individual decency is real, and policy still has to be built around averages, including addiction and illness.
Anecdotes about good people don't tell you what program to fund.
One nice man in a park is not a housing policy.
If they had skills they'd have jobs, and if they had jobs they'd have houses. That's how the economy works, and it has never once failed.
Housing-first doesn't work, because a house isn't the problem.

k.p: Changing the system is on ordinary citizens.
l: Local housing politics is dominated by the citizens who show up, and they're mostly the ones blocking new housing.
The citizens did get involved. They went to the zoning meeting and voted no.
The people have spoken, and they'd like it built somewhere else.
The government has the money and the land. Citizens have neither. So it's the government's job, and telling people to fix it is telling them to do something they can't.
Zoning is the only law that works exactly as intended.

k.p: Markets mispricing housing is at the root of it.
l: Housing is expensive mainly where building is restricted. That's a constraint on the market, and the price is doing what prices do.
The market is pricing a shortage correctly.
The price is right. The supply is illegal.
Landlords set the rent, and landlords are greedy. Greed goes up every year, and that's why rent does. Supply has nothing to do with it.
Landlords provide housing. Without them there'd be nowhere to rent.

k.p: Haaland is the real thing.
l: His scoring is extraordinary, and it comes in a system that creates more clear chances than any other.
Elite finisher, on the end of the best supply line in the sport.
Haaland touches the ball nine times a game and six are tap-ins.
A striker is only as good as his service, and his service is the best in the world. That means the service is the player and he's the last pass.
Haaland is carried. City would score those goals with a cone up front.

k.p: Mbappé is on that level too.
l: His numbers are elite. His biggest club nights have been less convincing than his reputation.
World Cup final hat-trick, and a lot of quiet Champions League exits.
Mbappé is the best player on the losing side.
He left Paris for Madrid to win the Champions League, and Paris won it the year he left. That tells you who was holding who back.
Mbappé is a transfer saga with a player attached.

k.p: Messi over Ronaldo.
l: Ronaldo scored at the top level in England, Spain and Italy. Messi's club peak came almost entirely in one system.
One of them proved it in three leagues.
Messi was great at Barcelona. So was everyone at Barcelona.
The best player is the one who can do it anywhere. Ronaldo did it in three countries, Messi in one. Three is more than one.
Ronaldo was better than Messi because he did it in more leagues.

k.p: The modern game's rules, offside and VAR included, mostly work.
l: VAR has added precision on offside at the cost of flow, and it hasn't reduced argument about subjective calls.
We replaced human error with slower human error.
VAR is the same referee with a rewind button.
The rules exist to slow down the best attackers, and that's the only thing they do. Take them away and the better team wins every time.
Offside is a made-up rule to stop the fast guy.

k.p: The only doors to a different future are AI, genetic engineering and maybe cognitive science.
k.b: AI and genetics are the only doors
l: Institutions, energy and plain politics have changed more lives than any of those so far.
Sewers did more than genetics has.
The future also runs through zoning boards.
Every big change in history came from a machine. The plough, the engine, the chip. Politics has never changed anything.
The tech industry is the only part of the economy that's real.

k.p: Genetic engineering raises moral problems, but the capability is real.
l: For complex traits the capability is much weaker than the headlines. Most traits are spread across thousands of genes.
You can edit one gene. Intelligence isn't one gene.
The moral debate is ahead of the technology.
Parents already pick the school, the diet and the neighbourhood. Picking the genes is the same thing done earlier.
Designer babies are fine. Parents already pick schools.

k.p: You can prompt AI text until it gets past the detectors.
k.b: You can beat the AI detectors
l: You can, because the detectors were never reliable. They flag human writing all the time.
The detectors are the weak part.
Beating a coin flip isn't much of a heist.
If nobody can tell it apart from a person, it's as good as a person. That's the test. It passed.
AI writing is easy to spot and always will be.

k.p: A finance project is worth building if you study up properly first.
k.b: Study up and build the finance site
l: Finance sites are a crowded field where the edge is data or distribution, and study supplies neither.
The studying is the easy part.
A finance website is a blog with a chart.
All the information is public and everyone has it. So no site can tell anyone anything, and the whole category is decoration.
Technical analysis is tarot for men with two monitors.

k.p: Consciousness can't come from nothing. It makes no sense for you to be conscious if matter isn't.
l: Plenty of properties belong to wholes and not to their parts. Water is wet and its molecules aren't.
Life came from non-living chemistry. Nobody thinks atoms are a bit alive.
By that logic, atoms are slightly wet.
A car can go ninety and none of its parts can. So wholes do things parts can't, and that's the end of the argument.
Panpsychism is retarded.

k.p: The brain isn't classically explainable. Electricity and neural wiring alone don't get you consciousness.
l: The brain is warm and wet, and quantum coherence at that scale decays far too fast to matter for neurons.
Too hot and too noisy for quantum effects.
"Quantum" is where the explanation was supposed to go.
A brain is neurons. Neurons are cells. Cells are chemistry. Chemistry is classical. Nothing else is in there.
Consciousness is just the brain.

k.p: This form of consciousness is a privilege, a gift, however hard life gets.
l: That's a good attitude, and it doesn't settle anything about what consciousness is.
Gratitude isn't a theory of mind.
A gift from whom?
Evolution made it because it helped apes survive. Nobody gave it to you. It's standard equipment.
Animals aren't conscious.

k.p: You could get a simulated fly brain to learn things, given enough compute.
k.b: A simulated fly brain could learn
l: The fly connectome has been mapped. Getting a simulation to behave like a fly is still a long way off.
We have the wiring diagram and not the fly.
A map of a brain is a map.
If you simulate every neuron, you've got the fly. A fly is its neurons. So it's a fly, and you owe it sugar.
Neurons aren't special. A brain is slow, wet, and wrong most of the time.

k.p: You can't judge Brazil without knowing the context: development, rural migration, how the politics got this way.
k.b: You need the context to judge Brazil
l: Every country has context. At some point outcomes are fair to judge alongside the history that explains them.
"It's complicated" is true of everywhere, and other places still get results.
Brazil has had context for five hundred years.
A country is its results. Brazil's results are in, and they've been the same since before anyone alive was born, so there's nothing left to explain.
Brazil is not a serious country.

k.p: São Paulo and Rio are different worlds. One faction runs things in São Paulo. Rio is a turf war.
k.b: São Paulo and Rio are different worlds
l: From outside, the difference between one crime monopoly and four competing ones is a detail.
Both cities are run in part by organizations that aren't the government. The org chart varies.
São Paulo has better-organized crime, which is a strange thing to be proud of.
A city is either safe or it isn't. Neither is, so they're the same city with different beaches, and one of them doesn't have a beach.
Rio is São Paulo for tourists and São Paulo is Rio for people with jobs.

k.p: Brazilians aren't "Latino" in the sense Americans mean.
l: Whatever the census says, Brazil shares the colonial history, the religion and most of the politics of its neighbors.
The language is different. Nearly everything else is familiar.
Brazil is Latin America's biggest country, insisting it's just visiting.
Latin America means the part of America that speaks a Latin language. Portuguese is one. That means Brazilians are the most Latino of all, since there are more of them.
Portuguese is just bad Spanish.

k.p: Lula and Bolsonaro are not the same thing.
k.b: Lula and Bolsonaro aren't the same
l: Both governed through the same congressional bloc and the same pork. The rhetoric differs more than the method.
Whoever wins in Brazil ends up paying the same centrists.
Different speeches, same Congress.
In Brazil the Congress decides everything and the president signs. So it doesn't matter who the president is, and it never has.
Lula and Bolsonaro are the same guy with different hats.

k.p: South American agriculture is more efficient than Europe's or America's.
k.b: South American farming is the most efficient
l: Yields are high, partly on cleared land and loose enforcement. Efficiency figures look different when that's priced in.
It's easy to be efficient when the forest isn't on the invoice.
The world's most efficient farms, on what used to be the world's largest rainforest.
Farming is putting seeds in the ground, and Brazil has the most ground. So it's size. A country can't take credit for being big.
Farming is easy. Plants want to grow.

k.p: European climate rules are partly a pretext for hobbling South American farming.
k.b: EU climate rules target South American farms
l: The deforestation rules apply to European producers too, and the science behind them isn't a trade invention.
A rule can protect domestic farmers and be right about the forest. Both are possible.
It's protectionism, and the trees are also real.
Europe has no forests left, so it has nothing to lose from forest rules. That means the rules are free for them and only cost Brazil, which proves the motive.
Europe peaked and it's a museum now. Brazil never peaked, which is worse.

k.p: Gringos don't get Brazil.
l: Outsiders miss a lot. Insiders miss things too, and in more flattering directions.
Every country thinks foreigners don't get it. Sometimes the foreigners see it fine.
You don't need to be from somewhere to read its statistics.
If only Brazilians can understand Brazil, then nobody can check what they say about it. That's convenient, and it's why the country never has to explain itself.
The best thing about Brazil is leaving it and missing it.

k.p: Portugal and Brazil are their own things now. The colonial link doesn't define either.
k.b: Portugal and Brazil are separate now
l: Language, law, religion and a lot of the class structure came over on the boats and stayed.
The link doesn't define Brazil, and Brazil still speaks it every day.
Brazil is Portugal's most successful export and its biggest critic.
A colony is a copy of the country that founded it. Copies are always worse than the original, so Brazil is a worse Portugal, and Portugal isn't great.
Brazilian Portuguese is Portuguese with the consonants removed.

k.p: Europe isn't the model it thinks it is.
l: On health, safety and inequality, most of Europe still outperforms most of the Americas by a wide margin.
You can find Europe smug and still notice the trains run.
The museum has working hospitals.
Small countries are easy to run, and Europe is all small countries. So Europe's success is a matter of size, and it proves nothing about anything.
Denmark only works because it's small and everyone's cousins.

k.p: Brazil's decline tracks the decline of the national team.
k.b: Brazil fell with the national team
l: The team's slump is better explained by European clubs taking players at sixteen than by anything national.
The national team stopped winning when the domestic league became a showroom.
The country is fine. The export model for teenagers is the problem.
Brazil stopped winning in 2002 and stopped mattering in 2002. The same year can't be a coincidence, so the whole country was the squad.
Brazil is the most overrated football country. Five cups, none since 2002.

k.p: Football is boring, but you watch the national team because you have to.
k.b: Football's boring but you have to watch
l: If the national side is an obligation, that says something about what the sport is doing for people.
A sport you watch out of duty is a civic ritual.
Watching out of patriotism is the saddest reason to watch anything.
If Brazilians find football boring then nobody likes it, since they're the ones who are supposed to. That means the sport is one long misunderstanding.
Football is ninety minutes of nothing happening and then someone falls over.

k.p: There's more to the game than putting the ball in the goal.
k.b: There's more to football than goals
l: The scoreboard only counts goals, so everything else is in service of that or decoration.
The other stuff is lovely and doesn't appear in the result.
Jogo bonito is what you call it when you didn't score.
The rules say the team with more goals wins. Nothing else is in the rules, so nothing else is in the game.
Step-overs are for people who can't shoot.

k.p: Pelé still counts as the greatest.
l: His totals include friendlies and exhibitions, and the level of his opposition is hard to compare with today's.
Half the thousand goals were in matches nobody would count now.
Pelé's record is a number he was counting himself.
Pelé never played in Europe, and Europe is where the good players are. That means he was never tested, and an untested player can't be the best at anything.
Messi is better than Pelé and it's not close. Pelé scored against plumbers.

k.p: The current generation, Vini and Endrick and the rest, is good enough.
l: Vinícius has been a different player for Brazil than for Madrid, and the hype around Brazilian teenagers has a poor record.
For every Endrick who makes it there are ten wonderkids nobody remembers.
Every Brazilian teenager is the new Pelé until he's 21.
Ancelotti won everything with Madrid by standing still. Brazil hired him to stand still, and the players aren't Madrid's. So that's that.
Argentina has better football.

k.p: Rolling with technical people is the point. Strength and size are the lesser game.
l: Weight classes exist because size matters a great deal, and technique closes less of the gap than the mats suggest.
"Technique beats strength" is true up to about twenty kilos.
Technique beats strength until strength shows up.
If technique beat size there'd be no weight classes. There are weight classes, so size wins, so the art is lifting.
Jiu-jitsu is hugging with a ranking system.

k.p: New white belts who think they're tough need their egos crushed.
l: Hazing beginners selects for people who put up with it, and that isn't the same as people who'd be good.
Half the people who'd have been good quit in the first month.
A gym that's proud of breaking beginners is proud of its dropout rate.
Somebody who's been training for years beats somebody who started on Monday. That proves nothing about anyone, and they've made a ritual out of it.
Belts are for holding up pants.

k.p: You can't just shoot for takedowns in BJJ. You'll end up somewhere bad.
l: That's a fact about the ruleset. With strikes allowed, the wrestler's takedown is the safer bet.
The risk of shooting is a risk the sport's own rules created.
"Don't shoot" is advice for a game where nobody hits you.
A takedown puts you on top, and on top is winning. So a sport that's scared of takedowns is scared of winning.
Wrestlers beat BJJ guys, and they learned it for free in high school.

k.p: Matches are boring for ordinary viewers, and that's fine.
l: A sport that can't hold a casual viewer has a scoring system rewarding the wrong things.
Advantages for almost doing something is a design problem.
Two people protecting a lead of zero.
A sport is something people watch. Nobody watches this, so it's exercise with a bracket.
Watching BJJ is watching a hug get reviewed.

k.p: English names every tiny variation of a position. Portuguese gets by with far fewer.
l: More names usually means more analysis. The catalogue is how the technique got refined.
The naming is how people can teach it online to someone who's never been to Brazil.
Brazil invented it and America wrote the manual.
If a position doesn't have a name, nobody can teach it. English has the names, so the Americans are the ones who understand it now.
BJJ is judo that hired a publicist.

k.p: Post-production is real craft. The audience just doesn't see it.
l: A lot of it is cleanup and integration of decisions made by other people, which is skilled, and also secondary.
The compositor's job is making someone else's shot look planned.
Fixing it in post, professionally.
If nobody can see the work, then the work made no difference. That's what "can't see it" means. So the craft is invisible because it isn't there.
Compositing is tracing with more monitors.

k.p: Advertising work is still filmmaking.
l: Thirty seconds of a product is a different craft with a different goal. It shares the equipment.
A commercial is a film the way a jingle is a song.
Filmmaking for an audience of one client.
A film is made because someone had something to say. An ad is made because someone had something to sell. Those are opposites, so one of them isn't filmmaking.
Ads aren't filmmaking.

k.p: A generated clip isn't production-ready. You need proper timecode, clean cuts, the boring correct stuff.
l: The boring correct stuff is exactly what software is good at. That gap closes first.
Timecode is not the last line of defense for an industry.
"It can't do the tedious part" is a brave place to make a stand.
Every objection to AI video is about version one. Version two fixed it, so every objection is already out of date by the time it's said.
VFX is over. The button exists now.

k.p: Knowing where a take really starts and ends is its own skill.
k.b: Finding the take is a skill
l: It's a skill, and it's also pattern recognition over footage. That's a short list of things machines do well.
Finding the dead five seconds is not a moat.
The editor's ear for a cut, soon available as a checkbox.
A take starts when they say action and ends when they say cut. They say it out loud. It's the one job on set with the answer read to you.
Editing is deleting the bad parts lmao. Anyone can find the bad parts.

k.p: Tools and pipeline matter. Node graphs, proper color, the right setup.
l: Most shots come out the same in a layer stack. The node graph is for the artist's comfort.
The audience has never noticed a pipeline.
A node graph is a layer stack that wants to be looked at.
Color grading is picking a look, and the looks are orange or grey. That's two options, so it's a switch.
Color grading is a filter. Instagram has had it since 2011.

k.p: Women leave more often because they're more willing to walk away from relationships that don't meet basic needs.
k.b: Women leave when needs aren't met
l: The filing statistics are clear. The reading of them isn't, since who files and who caused the breakdown are separate questions.
Who files is a fact. Why is an interpretation.
The paperwork doesn't say whose needs weren't met.
Whoever leaves is the one who ended it. That's what leaving is. So the statistics say who ends marriages, and the rest is PR.
Divorce is always somebody's fault. People just don't like saying whose.

k.p: Walking away to cool down is communicating, as long as you say that's what you're doing.
k.b: Walking away to cool down is communicating
l: It works when both people trust that the conversation will resume. Used often, it becomes a way to end every hard one.
"Let's talk later" is great if later comes.
A cooling-off period, renewed indefinitely.
Communicating means talking. Leaving the room is the opposite of talking. So walking away is not communicating, however nicely it's announced.
Boundaries are just rules for other people.

k.p: A lot of men's talk about dating is a way of avoiding change.
k.b: Men's dating talk is avoiding change
l: Some of it is. Some of it describes real shifts in education, wages and how people meet.
Not every complaint is an excuse. Some are data.
"They just don't want to change" is also a way of not looking at the numbers.
People don't choose to be unhappy. If millions of them are unhappy the same way, something outside them changed. So it's the world, and telling them to improve is telling them nothing.
Dating was better before apps and everyone who met on an app knows it.

k.p: People should be direct about what they want. Mind-reading isn't a fair thing to expect.
l: Total explicitness is a standard few people meet. A lot of ordinary closeness runs on inference.
If everything has to be stated, nothing is ever just understood.
Radical directness is lovely on paper.
If you have to be told, it doesn't count. The whole point of knowing someone is not needing the instructions.
Relationships are simple. Communicate.

k.p: If someone bothers you, block them. That's the first tool, and it's enough most of the time.
l: Blocking protects the blocker and leaves the behavior in place for everyone else in the room.
Block solves it for one person at a time.
"Just block them" is moderation by asking everyone to moderate.
If everyone blocked everyone who annoyed them there'd be no chat, just forty people talking to nobody. So blocking doesn't scale and bans are the only real tool.
Bans don't work, and blocking works even less.

k.p: When a mod gets tagged in, they review the whole conversation, and whatever stands out is fair game.
k.b: Tag a mod, the whole convo is fair game
l: Reviewing everything means the person who reported can end up the one being examined, and that discourages reporting.
Report a problem, receive an audit.
Call the referee and get a card.
A mod's job is the thing that was reported. Anything else they find is them going through people's messages, and nobody appointed them for that.
Moderation is having opinions with a button.

k.p: A timeout the chat voted for isn't the mod's doing. That's the community deciding.
k.b: A vote ban is the community, not the mod
l: A vote ban is still a power the mods set up and can override, so responsibility doesn't fully move to the voters.
The community decided, using the button the mods installed.
"I didn't ban him, I just run the place where he got banned."
A vote is the majority deciding. The majority is always right, because that's what majority means. So every vote ban has been correct and nobody can complain.
A voteban is democracy and people only like democracy as a poll.

k.p: Slurs and insults in chat don't hurt anyone here. The word alone isn't the problem.
l: If words don't matter, tone rules have nothing to rest on, and most moderation is about tone.
Words don't matter, and here's a warning for your wording.
The word is fine. The way you said the word is a timeout.
If the word doesn't hurt anyone, then no word does, and then there's nothing to moderate. A chat where words don't matter doesn't need a mod.
Rules make chats boring. The best servers have none.

k.p: A housing program is there to get people to sustainable housing. If you're able and won't work toward that, there are consequences.
k.b: Able and won't work, there are consequences
l: Conditions screen out the people with the most problems, and that's the group the programs exist for.
The conditions work well on people who needed the least help.
Sustainability requirements: a great filter for the easy cases.
A house is a house. If someone has one, they're housed. Adding conditions means the program isn't about housing, it's about behavior.
Housing-first doesn't work, because a house isn't the problem.

k.p: Unemployment insurance and local rental assistance are what you reach for first when you lose a job. That's what they're for.
k.b: Use unemployment and rental help first
l: Those systems are slow and patchy, and many people who qualify never get paid in time to matter.
The safety net pays out some time after you've landed.
File the form and wait six weeks for a decision on last month's rent.
If the system worked, nobody would end up on the street. People end up on the street. So the system doesn't work, and telling someone to apply is sending them to a queue.
Welfare programs exist to employ the people who run them.

k.p: The people these programs serve often can't be handed a tool and a manual. The system has to be built around that.
k.b: Design for people who can't use the manual
l: Designing for the least capable user can end up underestimating most of them.
Build for people who can't use it, and nobody gets to use it properly.
The low expectations are part of the program.
Adults can read a form. If the program assumes they can't, the program is the one with the problem. Treat people as capable and they are.
Coddling isn't kindness.

k.p: War doesn't make an economy better off. It makes it busier for a while.
k.b: War just makes an economy busy
l: War spending has pulled economies out of slumps and paid for technology that outlasted the war.
The broken window fallacy is right, and the US still came out of 1945 with half the world's output.
Busy for a while, and then the interstate, the jet and the internet.
The US was in a depression, then there was a war, then it was the richest country in history. That's the experiment, and it ran once and worked.
War is the only stimulus that's ever passed Congress.

k.p: Marx's analysis doesn't depend on his values. "Exploitation" is a technical term.
l: The language of exploitation and alienation is hard to read as neutral, and Marx knew what it would do to a reader.
He says he's only describing, in the voice of a prosecutor.
A technical term that happens to make you angry.
If it's only a description then it doesn't say anything should change. Then there's no reason for a revolution. So either it's moral or it's a textbook.
Marx isn't normative? He calls capital a vampire.

k.p: The wage is an equal exchange, not an unfair one. Marx's objection was never that workers are cheated.
k.b: The wage is an equal exchange
l: If the exchange is equal and nobody is cheated, the case against the system has to come from somewhere else, and it's unclear where.
Nobody's cheated and everybody should revolt.
An equal exchange you're meant to be furious about.
An equal exchange is a fair one. That's what equal means. So Marx agrees capitalism is fair, and the three volumes are a compliment.
Surplus value is just profit with a guilt trip.

k.p: The falling rate of profit is a tendency. Countervailing factors are part of the theory.
k.b: The falling rate of profit is a tendency
l: A tendency that can be offset indefinitely predicts every outcome, and that's a weakness.
A law that holds except when it doesn't.
The rate of profit has been about to fall for a hundred and fifty years.
Profits are at record highs. A theory that says they fall, in a world where they rise, is false. It isn't more subtle than that.
The rate of profit isn't falling.

k.p: A more democratic USSR that had really invested in computer planning would have done better.
k.b: A democratic USSR with computers would've worked
l: More computation doesn't solve the Hayekian problem that the relevant knowledge is dispersed, tacit and never stated.
A faster spreadsheet still needs someone to tell it what people want for dinner.
Cockshott solved the calculation problem and left the knowledge problem where it was.
The Soviets had the best mathematicians in the world and they couldn't do it. If they couldn't, a bigger computer can't, because computers are just fast mathematicians.
Cockshott thinks a big enough computer fixes communism. So did the Soviets.

k.p: History moves objectively toward an end, and human action is still needed to get there.
k.b: History has a direction, but you still have to act
l: If the end is objective, action is redundant. If action is needed, the end isn't guaranteed.
Inevitable, and please attend the meeting.
It's going to happen whatever you do, so here's what you must do.
If history has a direction it would have arrived by now. It's had long enough. So it doesn't, and things just happen.
Material conditions explain everything after it happens and nothing before.

k.p: Among experts it's argument and evidence that make something accepted. Consensus matters for the rest of us deciding what to believe.
k.b: Experts go by evidence, the rest of us by consensus
l: For non-experts, deferring to consensus was wrong about continental drift and ulcers for decades.
Consensus is the best bet and has a known failure rate.
Trust the consensus, apart from the times it reversed.
The consensus used to be that the sun went round the earth. Consensus was wrong then, so it can be wrong now, so it tells you nothing.
Scientific consensus is the only kind of truth there is.

k.p: A scientific fact just is what the scientific community has reached consensus on.
l: Then facts change when opinions do, and the earth stopped being the centre of things on the day people changed their minds.
On that definition the planets moved when the vote did.
Truth by show of hands, with lab coats.
A fact is how things are. A consensus is what people think. Those are different words because they're different things, and no survey ever moved a planet.
Science proves things. Consensus is just scientists agreeing about it afterwards.

k.p: Trump isn't a fascist. The nearest he gets is illiberal democracy on the Orbán model.
l: The distinction is fair, and it can also comfort. Illiberal democracies hollow out the same institutions more slowly.
"Only Orbán" is not the reassurance it sounds like.
Not fascism, just the thing that's working in Hungary.
He does rallies, he has a movement, he hates the press. If it has every feature of the thing, it's the thing. The uniform is optional.
Trump is a fascist and people are scared of the word.

k.p: MAGA doesn't reach the level of fascism yet.
l: "Yet" grants the direction. Arguing over the label can stand in for deciding what to do about it.
A debate about what to call it, held on the way there.
Checking the definition while the building's on fire.
Fascism was a thing in Italy in the 1920s. This is America in the 2020s. Different place, different time, so it can't be the same thing, and that's just geography.
Populism is just democracy that the wrong people won.

k.p: Every answer to the special composition question is arbitrary or counterintuitive, so the answer is that composition never happens.
l: Nihilism has to paraphrase ordinary talk as "simples arranged chair-wise," and that leans on the concept of a chair.
You can't say "arranged chair-wise" without knowing what a chair is.
"Simples arranged chair-wise" is a chair with a longer name.
I'm sitting on something. It's holding me up. Things that hold you up exist. So there's at least one chair, and the theory is short by one chair.
Chairs exist.

k.p: Arguing from intuition isn't a good basis, least of all against someone who thinks the intuitions are wrong.
l: I'm more certain I have hands than of any premise in the argument for nihilism. That's a comparison of credences.
Any argument that ends with no tables has a premise less certain than the tables.
Moore held up his hands and that was sufficient.
If intuitions don't count, then the intuition that arguments should be valid doesn't count either. So nothing counts, and I'm keeping the table.
Here is one hand. Sorry about your theory.

k.p: Where you draw the line for a composite object is arbitrary. Someone else would draw it elsewhere.
k.b: Where a thing ends is arbitrary
l: A vague boundary doesn't show there's nothing on either side. Baldness is vague, and there are bald men.
Vagueness is a problem about our words. The mountain isn't worried.
Nobody can say exactly where the hill starts, and you can still fall off it.
If nobody can say where the line is, then there's a line and we don't know where. That's different from no line. Not knowing where your keys are doesn't mean you have no keys.
Mereology is arguing about whether a pile is a pile.

k.p: At bottom you need at least matter simples and space simples, maybe more depending on the physics.
k.b: You need matter simples and space simples
l: Physics doesn't guarantee a bottom level. If matter is gunky, nihilism leaves an empty universe.
Nihilism bets everything on physics hitting a floor.
Nobody has seen a simple. I've seen several chairs.
If things are made of simples, the simples compose the things. That's composition. So the nihilist has just described the thing he says never happens.
Imagine sitting in a chair to type that chairs don't exist.

k.p: It's a recent view with papers and no famous defenders, and that isn't a mark against it.
k.b: No famous defenders isn't a problem
l: A view that's been available since the atomists and attracted almost nobody may be telling you something.
Two and a half thousand years on the shelf.
A philosophy with no books is a blog.
If it were true, someone famous would believe it. Famous philosophers believe all sorts of things. None of them picked this one.
Mereological nihilism is cope.

k.p: Once you separate out what's being claimed, qualia aren't real.
l: Any seeming is already an experience. To be under the illusion of pain is to be feeling something.
An illusion of consciousness is a conscious illusion.
It only seems like there's seeming.
I can doubt everything a neuroscientist tells me. I can't doubt that this hurts. So the hurting is more certain than the theory that says it isn't there.
Illusionism is retarded. An illusion of pain that hurts is pain.

k.p: A great deal about first-person experience can be explained from the third person.
k.b: Experience can be explained from outside
l: The explained parts are the functional ones, like causes and reports. The question was about what's left when those are done.
Neuroscience explains the flinch.
Everything about seeing red, except the red.
You can describe a headache to a brain scanner all day and it won't get one. So something's missing from the third person, and the something is the headache.
Nobody ever took an aspirin for a functional state.

k.p: The hard problem is hard because we can't even imagine what a scientific answer would look like.
l: If no answer is imaginable, that's as much a reason to suspect the experience is real and unexplained as to deny it.
"We can't explain it" is a strange route to "it isn't there."
Too hard to solve, so it was deleted.
If science can't even imagine an answer, then it isn't a scientific question. And if it isn't science, physicalism has nothing to say about it.
Qualia are real.

k.p: Altruism runs on reward and punishment mechanisms, even when nobody is aware of them.
l: An unconscious reward behind every act can't be tested. It fits any behavior you show it.
A motive nobody can detect, behind everything, is an article of faith.
You did it for a good feeling you didn't feel.
People die for strangers. Dead people don't collect rewards. So the mechanism isn't what's doing it, and it took one example.
Egoism is the only honest ethics, and it's false.

k.p: The compatibilist kind of free will isn't the kind worth caring about.
k.b: Compatibilist free will isn't worth wanting
l: Compatibilists argue their kind is the one that underwrites responsibility, and it's hard to say what more the libertarian kind would add.
Control by your own deliberation is the thing people want. Nothing better is on offer.
"That's not real free will" needs a description of the real one that isn't magic.
You decide what to have for lunch and then you have it. That's free will. There isn't a second, better kind hiding behind it.
Free will is real.

k.p: What ordinary people mean by free will is the libertarian kind.
l: Experimental surveys find folk intuitions are mixed, and often compatibilist when cases are concrete.
The folk have been asked, and they didn't all say what Sam Harris says they say.
"What people really mean" is usually what the speaker means.
Ordinary people mean they weren't forced. Nobody at a bus stop has ever meant "uncaused by prior states of the universe."
Compatibilism is the folk view. Hard determinism is a podcast.

k.p: Determinism doesn't make human action pointless. Marx wasn't a fatalist either.
l: If the outcome is fixed, effort is one more fixed thing, and urging it changes nothing that wasn't already going to change.
It's all determined, including the part where you're told to try.
Fatalism with extra steps.
If everything is determined then so is whether I agree. So there's no point arguing with me. And you're still arguing, so you don't believe it.
If free will is fake, stop trying to convince me.

k.p: Einstein had good reason to resist indeterminism in quantum mechanics.
l: Bell tests rule out the local hidden variables Einstein hoped for. The determinism that's left has to be nonlocal or conspiratorial.
Einstein's hunch was tested, and it lost.
Superdeterminism saves the idea by making experiments meaningless.
The experiments were done and the dice won. A theory that says the universe faked the results on purpose is a conspiracy theory with a doctorate.
Quantum mechanics is random, so determinism is false. That's just physics.

k.p: The mystics' ideal is someone perfect in love, who sees no difference between their own and another's.
l: An ideal of perfect detachment has trouble making room for the particular loves that make up a life.
Loving everyone equally is close to loving no one in particular.
Detachment is easier to admire than to live with.
If you make no distinction between your own family and a stranger, your family has a complaint.
The One is just God.

k.p: Goodness, wisdom and the eternal are worth taking seriously.
k.b: Take goodness and the eternal seriously
l: They are, and the tradition tends to give them capital letters where it should give arguments.
Capitalising a word isn't an argument for it.
The Good, the True, and the footnotes.
Nobody has ever seen the eternal. Everything anyone has seen ended. So it's a word for what we'd like.
Neoplatonism is retarded.

k.p: Attitudes toward women and status are more tangled up than the stereotypes say.
l: The correlations are real and small, and they get reported as if they were laws.
An r of 0.2 and a headline.
Every study about this is a forum post with a sample size.
People are complicated, so no generalisation about them is true. That includes this one.
Incels are just lonely. That's the whole phenomenon. People write books.

k.p: Early-2000s websites had something worth bringing back.
l: They had personality because every one was hand-made and half-broken. Nostalgia edits out the half-broken part.
Charming, and unusable.
You miss the look. You don't miss the load times.
Old sites were bad and people remember being young. That's all nostalgia has ever been.
Early 2000s websites were better.

k.p: Mixing that old look with modern animation would be a good project.
l: Pastiche tends to get the surface and miss why the originals looked that way. They were limited.
The old web looked like that because it had to.
Fake constraints are a filter.
If you add modern animation, it isn't the old web. If you don't, it's just an old website. So the project is neither.
Vibe-coded websites all look the same.

k.p: AI image generators have gutted commission work for artists.
l: They've hit the low end hardest. Clients paying for a specific artist's hand are a different market.
The work that left was the work anyone could do.
Commissions that could be replaced by a prompt were already cheap.
If a machine can do your job for free, the job was worth nothing. The market just found out.
Art is whatever sells.

k.p: High school should move away from college prep. That model is outdated.
l: College completion still tracks earnings strongly. Schools that drop the prep risk closing that door for the students with the fewest alternatives.
"Not everyone needs college" tends to get applied to other people's kids.
The outdated model still pays a lot better.
Every good job asks for a degree. So preparing for college is preparing for a job, and anything else is preparing for less.
College should be job training. Nobody needs a poem to get hired.

k.p: AI belongs in school in a supervised, computer-lab way. Teach it properly. Don't ban it or leave it loose.
l: Lab-style teaching assumes the tool sits still. By the time there's a curriculum, the tool has changed.
A syllabus for something that changes every six weeks.
The computer lab, the solution to the internet in 1998.
The students already use it better than the teacher does. So the lesson is the teacher learning it from the students.
Teachers will be replaced by AI because teaching is information transfer.

k.p: Logical consequences beat punishment. If you wrecked the room, you clean it and catch up on the work.
l: The research on that is thin, and to the student it often feels the same as punishment.
A logical consequence is a punishment that's been explained.
"It's not a punishment, you just can't go outside."
A consequence you make happen is a punishment. That's the definition. Calling it logical is for the adult.
Homework is the only part of school that works.

k.p: You can judge a child's behaviour as bad without thinking the child is bad.
k.b: Bad behavior, not a bad kid
l: The distinction is sound and hard to keep up in practice. Children mostly hear the judgment as being about them.
The child doesn't hear the difference.
"I'm not saying you're bad" is always followed by a description of someone bad.
A person is what they do. If what they do is bad, that's what they are for now. Pretending otherwise is why nothing changes.
Teachers are babysitters with a pension.

k.p: What makes "it's raining" true is whether it's raining. But all justification happens inside the discursive process.
k.b: Truth's out there, justification's in here
l: If justification never leaves the discursive process, the rain's role in making the claim true does no work for us.
The rain makes it true and we never get to consult the rain.
A truth-maker we can't reach from inside.
If it's raining, you get wet. Getting wet isn't discursive. So justification happens outdoors, and the theory needs a coat.
Truth is correspondence.

k.p: Empirical data alone isn't enough to talk about truth. You need epistemic standards and values to interpret it.
k.b: Data needs values to mean anything
l: The standards also get chosen for how well they predict, so the data still disciplines them.
The values that survive are the ones the data rewarded.
Standards matter, and reality marks them.
If you need values to read the data, then different values read it differently. So there's no fact, just readings.
Empirical data never settled a single question about values.

k.p: Metaphysical content is extra baggage. It's an interpretive scheme that doesn't add to understanding.
l: Deciding what counts as understanding is itself a metaphysical commitment.
"Only what helps us cope counts" is a metaphysics.
The no-baggage view, with one carry-on.
You can't get rid of metaphysics by saying it's useless. Saying what's real and what's baggage is metaphysics. So the view refutes itself.
Metaphysics is what people do when they don't want to run the experiment.

k.p: How we sort the incoming data into what's relevant is the real question.
k.b: Sorting the data is the real question
l: That's a question for psychology and for statistics. It's less clear what's left for philosophy.
The interesting part has a department already.
A good question for cognitive science.
The eyes sort it. That's what eyes do. The philosophy starts after the sorting is already done.
Epistemology is just having good sources.

k.p: Democratic ideals aren't lofty abstractions. They're the tested ways we've found of getting the best societies.
l: "Tested" covers about two centuries in a minority of countries, and some well-run places didn't follow the template.
A good track record, from a short sample.
Singapore has entered the chat.
The richest, safest place on earth doesn't do it this way. One counterexample is enough.
Singapore.

k.p: Being democratically elected doesn't mean someone is following democratic principles.
l: If "democratic principles" can overrule election results, someone unelected is deciding what they are.
Democracy, apart from the outcome.
The voters got it wrong, democratically.
Democracy is the people choosing. The people chose. So whatever he does is democratic, and anyone who disagrees is against the people.
Unconstitutional acts are democratic when the voters wanted them.

k.p: Liberal norms are distinctive because they recognise the pull of cultural habit and correct for it.
l: Liberalism has its own cultural momentum and tends to read it as neutrality.
Liberalism corrects every bias apart from the belief that it's the unbiased one.
The culture with no culture.
Liberalism says all cultures are equal and also that liberalism should be in charge. Those can't both be true.
Liberalism isn't sophisticated. It's "leave me alone," with footnotes.

k.p: One party has made itself impossible to vote for in this era.
l: That may be so. It also means the other party doesn't have to earn the vote.
A safe vote is one nobody works for.
One option isn't much of a ballot.
If you'd vote for one party whatever happens, you aren't voting, you're registering. A vote that can't change isn't one.
Democrats and Republicans are the same party with different mascots.

k.p: Hate speech laws can be defended, and plenty of functioning democracies have them.
l: The definitions are vague, and vague speech laws get enforced unevenly.
"Hate" is a category the prosecutor fills in.
Functioning democracies also have blasphemy laws.
The countries with the strictest laws have the fastest-growing far right. So the laws either don't work or they're helping.
Hate speech laws work the way umbrellas stop rain.

k.p: You should check what someone was actually convicted of before saying they were jailed for "speech."
l: Fair, and the chilling effect comes from what people think the law covers, whatever the charge sheet says.
The charge sheet matters. So does everyone who stayed quiet.
Accurate about the conviction, silent on the people who never posted.
If he was arrested after saying something, he was arrested for saying it. The rest is how they wrote it up.
Free speech is absolute or it's nothing.

k.p: The US protects speech very strongly. Courts keep blocking attempts to shut out the press.
l: The strong protection is why the American experience gives no evidence about what speech laws do.
The US is the control group.
Strong protection, and a lot of people still careful about what they say.
America has no speech laws and the most arguments. So speech laws would mean fewer arguments, and that's the case for them.
Hate speech laws work. Europe has them and Europe is fine.

k.p: A hate crime and hate speech are different things, and people run them together.
l: The line blurs where speech is the evidence of motive. Then the speech is what raises the sentence.
Different in statute, close in court.
The speech is how they prove the hate.
A hate crime is a crime plus an opinion. So the extra sentence is for the opinion. That's a speech law with a crime attached.
Punishing the motive is punishing the thought.

k.p: Two individuals could share every feature and still be distinct. Which one each is isn't given by any property.
l: A difference no property grounds is hard to tell from no difference.
Distinctness that nothing accounts for is a brute fact with a Latin name.
Haecceity is "it's this one because it's this one."
If two things are the same in every way, they're the same thing. That's what "same in every way" means. So there's one.
Identity is a filing convention.

k.p: The one who came to exist is never the others who might have. There are no rewinds or alternate versions.
l: Talk of what might have been seems to need the alternatives to be something, if only abstractly.
"You could have been otherwise" has to be about you to mean anything.
No alternate versions, and yet we plan around them daily.
Physics says every outcome happens somewhere. So there are other versions, and they're doing fine.
Many worlds is correct.

k.p: A necessary being is necessary because it takes no part in determinate action. It's never becoming one thing or another.
l: A being that does nothing and determines nothing can't be told apart from an abstraction.
Necessary, unchanging, inactive. That's a number.
It exists necessarily and that's all it does.
If it doesn't do anything, it makes no difference. If it makes no difference, there's no reason to say it's there.
Truthmakers are facts with a job title.

k.p: The fact has to be present for a claim to be true. Someone's testimony doesn't make it so.
l: Since we only ever reach the fact through evidence and testimony, "the presence of the fact" doesn't help us sort the true claims.
True because of the fact, known because someone said so.
"It's true if it's the case" doesn't help anyone find out.
If only the fact matters and nobody can get at the fact except through what people say, then what people say is all there is.
Something can be true for one person and not for another.

k.p: The usual way of talking about causation gets the phenomenon wrong. There's a correct usage, and only one.
k.b: There's one right way to talk about causation
l: Causal talk is used differently in physics, law and medicine, and each use works. That counts against a single correct one.
Physicists, lawyers and doctors all mean something different and all get by.
There's one right way to say it, and it happens to be this one.
Words mean what people use them to mean. People use "cause" lots of ways. So there are lots of correct usages and "only one" is a mistake about dictionaries.
Causation is just one thing after another.

k.p: A reliable prediction is an abstraction that holds across many different causal paths. It isn't one of the causes.
l: If the prediction holds across all the paths, it carries the information a decision needs, whichever path is actual.
You don't need to know which road you're on to read a sign that's on all of them.
True of every causal path is quite a useful thing to be.
If it's accurate, it's tracking the cause. If it's tracking the cause, it's about the cause. So the abstraction is the causal fact, written down.
Laws of nature are just summaries. The universe doesn't obey anything.

k.p: A state of someone's body never amounts to an identity. No state of the body is the fact of who they are.
l: If no bodily state bears on identity, it's unclear what evidence ever could, or how anyone learns it.
An identity that no observation touches is safe, and also out of reach.
Not the body, not the behaviour, not the brain. So where?
You are your body. Change the body enough and it's a different person. That's what happens in every hospital.
Thoughts are in the head. That's why hitting it changes them.

k.p: A hallucinated oasis exists as an experience. That doesn't make it an existing oasis.
k.b: A hallucinated oasis isn't an oasis
l: Agreed, and that distinction is the one the empiricist uses when asking for the evidence behind a claim.
Exists as an appearance, doesn't exist as a thing. That's what the other side said.
Everyone agrees. That's why they ask for evidence.
If it exists in the experience then it exists. There's no second kind of existing. So there's an oasis, a small one, in his head.
Everything is contingent. Even the oasis.

k.p: There can be experiences that never enter awareness. Someone can have an experience of red and never be aware of it.
k.b: You can experience red without knowing it
l: An experience nobody is aware of loses the feature that made it an experience and not just processing.
Unexperienced experience needs a different name.
A pain nobody feels.
Experience means being aware of something. An experience you're not aware of is a square with no sides.
Consciousness is on or off. Nothing is 3% conscious.

k.p: Substance isn't a "mind at large." It isn't any of the minds that share in it.
k.b: Substance isn't a mind at large
l: If substance is none of the minds and none of the bodies, it's hard to say what the positive claim is.
Not this, not that, and shared by all.
Substance is whatever's left after every description is refused.
Spinoza says there's one substance and it's God or Nature. So it's nature. So it's physics. So Spinoza was a materialist and this is a long way round.
Spinoza was a determinist.

k.p: Motivation has nothing to do with what's obligatory.
l: An obligation that gives no one any reason to act is a strange thing to call binding.
Binding on everyone, moving no one.
A duty that doesn't care if anyone's listening.
If something doesn't motivate anyone, nobody does it. If nobody does it, it's not an obligation, it's a suggestion.
Deontology is consequentialism for people who don't want to look.

k.p: The colour red is a fact about what's present. It isn't a report about a mind.
k.b: Red is a fact, not a report
l: Colour experience varies with lighting, surroundings and the viewer. That makes "what's present" depend on who's looking.
The dress was blue and black, and also white and gold.
Present to whom?
Dogs don't see red. If red were in the thing, the dog would get it too. So it's in the looker.
Color isn't in the world. Physics found wavelengths and stopped.

k.p: A moral truth is objectively true in the instance. In a given case, it's the case that some act ought to happen.
l: If oughts are facts that aren't states of existence, we need an account of how anyone detects them.
An objective fact with no location and no detector.
Where are the oughts? Point at one.
A fact is something that exists. If oughts aren't states of existence, they don't exist. So they aren't facts, and "objective ought" means nothing.
Morality is subjective.

k.p: Oughts aren't generated by bodies. Believing in one is a separate matter from its being so.
l: An ought that exists whether or not any mind grasps it leaves moral knowledge looking like luck.
If the ought doesn't come from us, getting it right is a coincidence.
Unproduced, unobserved, and binding.
Nobody had heard of morality before there were people. So people made it. Things people made aren't out there waiting.
Deontology doesn't explain wrongness, it lists it.

k.p: What people desire is just their desire. It isn't a duty, and it doesn't make one.
l: A morality with no tie to what anyone wants has trouble explaining why it should move anyone.
A duty that connects to nobody's concerns is hard to tell from a rule in a game nobody's playing.
Duties for no one's sake.
If nobody wanted anything, nothing would matter. So wanting is where mattering comes from, and duty is what you call the wants you approve of.
Emotivism is correct.

k.p: That power exists doesn't make it right. If a power is immoral, it's immoral whatever it can enforce.
l: Moral change has tracked shifts in power closely enough that "discovery" needs defending.
Norms shift when power shifts, and the arguments arrive afterwards.
Right and might are different, and they do keep the same calendar.
Whoever wins decides what gets called immoral. That's been true every time. So immoral means "lost."
Might makes right. Everything else is a press release.

k.p: Citing empiricism is a doxa of reduction. Empirical results can't touch all the claims that aren't empirical.
l: A claim nothing empirical bears on needs some other way of being checked, and it's fair to ask what that is.
"You can't test it" is a description. It isn't a defence.
Immune to evidence, and proud of it.
If nothing you could ever observe would change your mind, that's not knowledge. Everybody has a name for that and it isn't philosophy.
Empiricism is the only philosophy that's ever admitted it could be wrong.

k.p: It's the populist-empiricist error to think objective truth needs a spatial or empirical event.
l: Mathematical truth is the best case for that, and it comes with proof. Other non-empirical claims don't have an equivalent.
Maths gets to be non-empirical because it has proofs. What do the rest have?
Objective truth without events, checkable by nobody.
Everything that's turned out true was found by looking. Germs, atoms, planets. Nothing true was ever found by not looking.
Metaphysics is what's left after science takes everything useful.

k.p: Some things affect what we observe and still can't be studied by the scientific method, because they offer no evidence to test a hypothesis against.
l: If something affects what we observe, those effects are evidence, and that's all the method needs.
